AD.plates: White plate with black characters and a small colour coat of arms on the left; no blue EU strip. The number is usually a letter followed by digits.
AD.roads: Steep two-lane mountain roads with hairpins, white markings and long runs of metal crash barrier. There are no motorways; the main routes are signed CG followed by a number.
AD.built: Dark slate roofs and rough stone walls on older Pyrenean buildings, with tall modern hotel and apartment blocks packed tightly into a narrow valley floor. Shopping streets are unusually dense with electronics, perfume and tobacco shops.
AD.nature: Very steep slopes of pine and birch, bare rock and scree above the treeline, and snow on the tops for much of the year.
AD.extra: Signage is in Catalan, so expect Carrer, Avinguda and Benvinguts rather than Spanish or French wording. Prices are in euros and duty-free advertising is highly visible.

AE.plates: White plates with black characters, with the emirate name in Arabic and English at the top and a code letter or number; each emirate uses its own layout and some carry a coloured band or emblem on the left.
AE.roads: Drives on the right. Enormous multi-lane highways with green direction signs in Arabic above English, blue signs for local routes, fresh white markings, and continuous concrete or steel barriers in the median.
AE.poles: Highway lighting is on tall tapered steel columns; distribution cabling is largely underground in cities, with steel poles on desert roads.
AE.built: Sand-coloured rendered villas with flat roofs and high boundary walls in regular blocks, dense towers in Dubai and Abu Dhabi, and low-rise concrete shop rows with Arabic and English fascia signs.
AE.nature: Flat gravel plains and orange-red sand dunes inland, sabkha salt flats near the coast, and heavily irrigated verges planted with date palms, oleander and clipped shrubs fed by visible drip lines.
AE.extra: Sand drift across the hard shoulder and the sharp line between irrigated green verge and raw desert are reliable cues. Large white Nissan Patrols and Toyota Land Cruisers dominate traffic.

AF.plates: White plates with black characters, the numerals and province name in Perso-Arabic script, often with a smaller Latin transliteration. Layouts vary and older hand-painted plates are still seen.
AF.roads: Drives on the right. Outside the ring road most surfaces are gravel or packed earth with no markings at all; paved sections have faded white lines and almost no guardrail.
AF.built: Flat-roofed mud brick and concrete houses inside high blank compound walls, with metal gates opening straight onto the street. Bazaars are lines of small open-fronted shops under corrugated awnings.
AF.nature: Bare tan and grey mountains with almost no tree cover, dusty gravel plains, and lines of tall poplars marking irrigated fields and riverbeds.
AF.extra: Imagery is extremely scarce and mostly from moving vehicles. Toyota Corolla estates and white Toyota HiAce vans dominate traffic.

AG.plates: White plates with black characters and a leading letter marking the vehicle class, such as A for private and T for taxi.
AG.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Roads are narrow and frequently unmarked away from St John's, with white edge lines at best, shallow concrete drainage channels at the verge and painted speed humps through villages.
AG.poles: Wooden utility poles carrying only a handful of lines are the norm.
AG.built: Low concrete-block houses painted in strong colours with corrugated metal or hipped roofs, some older timber houses with louvred shutters, and cut-stone ruins of colonial sugar mills standing in open fields.
AG.nature: Antigua is dry and low: acacia and thorn scrub, sea grape, tamarind and scattered cactus over pale limestone ground, with very little tall forest. Barbuda is flatter, sandier and scrubbier still.
AG.extra: English signage with East Caribbean dollar prices and .ag addresses. Right-hand-drive Japanese used cars are overwhelmingly common.

AI.plates: White plates with black characters carrying the name Anguilla.
AI.roads: Drives on the left, although almost every vehicle is a left-hand-drive American import. Narrow flat sealed roads with British-style signage, several roundabouts and frequent speed bumps.
AI.poles: Wooden poles heavily guyed against hurricanes, carrying thick bundles of cable and drum transformers.
AI.built: Low concrete houses in pastel colours with flat or shallow metal roofs and hurricane shutters, with many half-finished concrete structures showing exposed rebar.
AI.nature: Extremely flat and dry, with low scrub, acacia, sea grape and agave, white sand and vividly turquoise water often visible, and no hills anywhere.
AI.extra: Salt ponds behind the beaches and goats wandering the verges. US dollars and American vehicles combined with left-hand traffic.

AL.plates: White plate front and rear with a blue strip on the left carrying AL, and a distinctive red vertical band down the right-hand edge. Format is two letters, three digits, two letters.
AL.roads: Road markings are white and often worn or entirely absent on secondary roads. Surfaces swing between smooth new tarmac on the main corridors and broken, patched or unsealed lanes in villages; kerbs and roadside walls are frequently painted white.
AL.poles: Plain grey concrete poles are the norm outside cities, usually carrying a messy bundle of low-slung cables with improvised joins.
AL.built: Half-finished houses of red hollow brick with bare concrete frames and rebar sticking up from the roof are everywhere. Tirana and other towns have communist blocks repainted in strong blocks of colour, and small dome-shaped concrete bunkers still sit in fields and verges.
AL.nature: Mediterranean scrub and olive groves on the coastal plain, bare grey karst limestone inland, with red-brown soil and scattered cypress.
AL.extra: An unusually high share of the traffic is older Mercedes-Benz saloons. Shopfront words like Lavazh (car wash), Furrë Buke (bakery) and Ujë are common, and Albanian uses ë and ç heavily.

AM.plates: White plates with black characters and a narrow blue band on the left carrying AM. Format is two digits, two letters, three digits.
AM.roads: Drives on the right. Blue direction signs with white text on main roads, green on the few motorway sections, with worn white markings and frequent stretches of patched asphalt and potholes.
AM.poles: Mostly grey concrete poles, square or round in section, with older steel lattice pylons on the edges of towns.
AM.built: Buildings faced in pink, orange and cream volcanic tuff are the signature look, alongside grey Soviet-era apartment blocks with enclosed balconies.
AM.nature: Dry treeless highland grassland and volcanic rock, with apricot and walnut trees around villages and snow-capped Ararat visible to the south-west on clear days.
AM.extra: Lada Nivas, old GAZ and UAZ vehicles and imported Opels are common. Carved khachkar stone crosses and small stone chapels appear at roadsides.

AO.plates: White plates front and rear with black characters, grouped as two letters, four digits and two letters. Newer issues carry a blue band on the left with the flag and the letters ANG.
AO.roads: Drives on the right. Recently rebuilt trunk roads have crisp white markings and black-and-white painted kerbstones, while signage is in Portuguese and most secondary roads are unmarked earth.
AO.poles: Square-section concrete poles are usual, with older wooden poles in the countryside and tall steel lighting columns along the new Chinese-built highways.
AO.built: Pastel-rendered Portuguese colonial buildings with tiled roofs in the old centres, surrounded by breeze-block houses with corrugated iron roofs; Luanda sets glass towers against sprawling musseque shanties.
AO.nature: Red-orange lateritic soil, dry miombo woodland and baobabs inland, dense green palm and bush along the coast, and stark desert scrub in the far south.
AO.extra: Blue-and-white Toyota Hiace candongueiro minibuses are everywhere, and Unitel and Movicel advertising is painted directly onto kiosks and compound walls.

AQ.extra: There are no settlements, public roads or vehicle registrations; the only ground-level views are at research stations, where you would see prefabricated huts raised on stilts, tracked snow vehicles and flagged route markers across bare ice or rock.

AR.plates: Mercosur plates: white with a blue strip across the top reading ARGENTINA, in a two letters, three digits, two letters format. The previous generation is plain white with three black letters and three digits, and some older vehicles still carry black plates with white characters.
AR.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Centre lines are usually white, with yellow kept for no-overtaking sections and painted kerbs. Rural routes have white-painted delineator posts, cable or W-beam guardrail, and long straight sightlines across the pampas.
AR.poles: A mix of square-section reinforced concrete poles in towns and creosoted wooden poles across the countryside, with slim concrete poles carrying long rural distribution runs.
AR.built: Single-storey rendered brick houses with flat or shallow roofs, painted white or pastel, built hard against the pavement; grid-plan towns with rolling metal shutters on the shopfronts.
AR.nature: Flat grassland and crop fields across the pampas, broken by planted rows of poplar and eucalyptus as windbreaks. Dry cactus scrub in the north-west, the Andes on the western horizon, and southern beech and arid steppe in Patagonia.
AR.extra: Spanish with Rioplatense usage, PARE stop signs and YPF filling stations. Roadside shrines to Gauchito Gil, marked by clusters of red flags and red-painted shelters, are a very reliable Argentine cue.

AS.plates: US-sized plates reading American Samoa, usually with a tropical beach and palm graphic.
AS.roads: Drives on the right, in direct contrast to independent Samoa just across the water. The main coast road has US-style signage, yellow centre lines, white edge lines and very low speed limits posted in miles per hour.
AS.poles: American-pattern wooden utility poles with drum transformers and multiple crossarms.
AS.built: Concrete houses with metal roofs, American-style school and government buildings with covered walkways, very large churches, and open fale with rows of pillars.
AS.nature: Extremely steep, densely forested volcanic ridges dropping almost vertically into the sea, coconut palms along the shore and a deep drowned harbour at Pago Pago.
AS.extra: Yellow American school buses, US highway sign shapes and mph limits, and the tuna cannery complex at the head of Pago Pago harbour.

AT.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and A, then the district code, a small national seal flanked by red-white-red bars, then the registration. A thin red line runs around the edge of the plate.
AT.roads: White markings; motorway direction signs are blue and lesser roads use white signs with black text. Roadside delineator posts are white with a black cap, and alpine stretches add tall red-and-white snow poles.
AT.poles: Distribution is often buried in built-up areas; in the countryside you see plain wooden poles and slim square concrete posts.
AT.built: Rendered houses in cream, ochre and pale green with wide overhanging eaves, timber balconies and shallow roofs in the alpine areas. Village churches typically have a slim tower topped by a copper onion dome.
AT.nature: Dark spruce plantations on steep slopes, close-mown green pasture with hay barns, and grey limestone crags above.
AT.extra: Gasthof and Gasthaus signs hang from wrought-iron brackets. Small wooden roadside crucifixes and shrines are frequent, and windscreens carry the rectangular motorway vignette sticker.

AU.plates: Reflective white plates with black or coloured characters and the state or territory name printed along the bottom, with no country code. New South Wales and Victoria use three letters then three digits, and Queensland plates carry maroon lettering.
AU.roads: Drives on the left. Sealed roads have a broken white centre line and continuous white edge lines, and yellow diamond warning signs are standard; inland, long unsealed roads run through bright red or orange dirt.
AU.poles: Weathered wooden poles in older suburbs and rural areas. South Australia is given away instantly by Stobie poles, made of two steel joists with a concrete slab between them.
AU.built: Single-storey brick-veneer houses with tiled or corrugated Colorbond steel roofs, metal fences and a carport; in the tropical north, timber Queenslander houses stand raised on stumps with wide verandahs.
AU.nature: Eucalypts of every kind with pale trunks and hanging leaves, dry straw-coloured grass, spinifex and saltbush in the interior, and wet rainforest with tree ferns along the eastern ranges.
AU.extra: White roadside guide posts with a red reflector on the left and white on the right line the verges. Route markers are white shields for national highways, and kangaroo and wombat warning signs are common.

AW.plates: White plates with black characters reading Aruba, often with the One Happy Island slogan along the bottom.
AW.roads: Drives on the right. Smooth sealed roads with Dutch-influenced signage and markings, plenty of roundabouts, and a fast coastal road linking Oranjestad to the hotel strip.
AW.poles: Concrete poles in town and wooden poles in the countryside, with wind turbines visible on the windward north-east coast.
AW.built: Dutch colonial stepped gables painted in strong pastels along the Oranjestad waterfront, and elsewhere low concrete houses with tiled roofs and gravel or cactus gardens.
AW.nature: Arid and almost treeless, with divi-divi trees permanently bent to the south-west by the trade wind, columnar cactus, aloe and scattered boulder fields.
AW.extra: Dutch text on official signs alongside Papiamento and English. The constant lean of the divi-divi trees is the single best Aruba cue.

AX.plates: Finnish-style white plates with black characters, but with a blue side strip carrying the Aland flag and the code AX instead of the Finnish FIN.
AX.roads: Drives on the right. Quiet two-lane asphalt with Finnish road furniture, including the yellow diamond priority sign and elk warning triangles, but with every sign in Swedish only rather than bilingual Finnish and Swedish.
AX.poles: Slender wooden poles, often slightly leaning, running along the edge of forest and field.
AX.built: Timber houses painted in red ochre falu paint with white window trim, large barns, and small stone or timber churches with separate bell towers.
AX.nature: Pine and spruce forest with birch, smooth pink granite outcrops, flat low-lying land, reed-fringed shores and frequent glimpses of sea between the trees.
AX.extra: Small ferry ramps and yellow road-ferry signs appear constantly because the territory is an archipelago. Finnish-style road markings combined with Swedish-only text is the decisive combination.

AZ.plates: White plates with black characters and a blue band on the left showing AZ and the flag. Format is a two-digit region code, two letters and three digits.
AZ.roads: Drives on the right. Main routes are unusually smooth and wide with crisp white markings, blue and green direction signs, and long runs of grey W-beam guardrail.
AZ.poles: Grey concrete poles, often square with a tapering profile, plus steel lattice towers along the main highways.
AZ.built: Baku uses pale cream limestone facades; elsewhere expect single-storey brick and cinder block houses with shallow metal roofs behind low walls.
AZ.nature: Semi-arid steppe and scrub on the Caspian lowlands, giving way to green wooded foothills of the Greater Caucasus in the north.
AZ.extra: Tree trunks and kerbs are frequently painted white, and national flags and portraits appear on roadside hoardings. Ladas share the road with newer Hyundais.

BA.plates: White plate with a blue strip and BIH on the left; the number uses only characters shared by the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets, so you see A, E, J, K, M, O and T in a pattern like A12-B-345.
BA.roads: Narrow winding roads through steep valleys, white markings often faded, and frequent short tunnels and rockfall netting. Motorway direction signs are green and other main roads blue, as elsewhere in the former Yugoslavia.
BA.poles: Grey concrete poles, square or round in section, are the usual carrier; older wooden poles survive on minor village lines.
BA.built: Red pantile roofs over rendered or bare block walls, with many unfinished houses. Bullet and shell damage is still visible on some facades, and skylines mix slim minarets with Orthodox and Catholic bell towers.
BA.nature: Karst limestone with bare grey outcrops, dense beech and black pine forest, and very clear turquoise rivers in deep gorges.
BA.extra: Signs often appear in both Latin and Cyrillic, with one script sometimes painted over. Red skull-and-crossbones landmine warning signs still appear on rural verges, and roadside ćevabdžinica and pekara signs are common.

BB.plates: White plates with black characters and a leading letter coding the class, with Z used for public service vehicles.
BB.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Roads are narrow but well surfaced, with kerbs, roundabouts and British-pattern direction signs, often running between coral stone walls and sugar cane on both sides.
BB.poles: Wooden utility poles carrying dense bundles of overhead cable, frequently leaning and set close to the carriageway.
BB.built: Small timber chattel houses with steep gabled roofs, jalousie windows and fretwork trim sit alongside rendered concrete bungalows; coral limestone blockwork and painted rum shops at crossroads.
BB.nature: Gently rolling coral limestone with extensive sugar cane, mahogany stands, casuarina along the coast and no high mountains anywhere on the island.
BB.extra: English signage and .bb addresses. Brightly painted ZR route minibuses playing loud music are a constant presence on main roads.

BD.plates: Private vehicles use white plates with black Bengali characters in two lines, with the district name on top; commercial vehicles use green plates. Many rickshaws and older vehicles carry hand-painted numbers.
BD.roads: Drives on the left. Narrow two-lane highways with faded white centre lines, low concrete kerbs, and black-and-white striped posts on bends; direction signs are green or blue with Bengali above English.
BD.poles: Square tapered concrete poles carrying tangled bundles of cable, with bamboo props and lattice steel towers in places.
BD.built: Red brick buildings and brick kilns with tall chimneys, unrendered concrete frames with exposed rebar, and vast areas of corrugated tin sheeting walls and roofs.
BD.nature: Flat waterlogged delta of rice paddy, jute and ponds, with banana, betel nut palm, jackfruit and mango trees crowding every village.
BD.extra: Cycle rickshaws with painted rear panels, green CNG auto-rickshaws in cages, and buses and trucks covered in dense hand-painted decoration. Crowds of people are almost always in frame.

BE.plates: White plate with dark crimson-red characters, a blue EU strip and B. The rear plate is reflective and the front one is often smaller and duller; older plates carry the same red lettering without the EU strip.
BE.roads: Motorways are frequently surfaced in concrete slabs with visible transverse joints, and are lined with orange-tinted lighting columns that stay lit at night. Markings are white, motorway signs blue, and other direction signs white with black text.
BE.poles: Overhead lines are mostly gone from main roads; where they remain the poles are slim concrete, and street lighting usually sits on its own dedicated column.
BE.built: Continuous ribbon development of brick houses strung along rural roads, each one a different height, roofline and brick shade from its neighbour. Brown and dark red brick dominates, with stepped gables in the older Flemish towns.
BE.nature: Flat to gently rolling arable land in the north, rows of poplars along field edges, and beech-dominated woodland in the hillier Ardennes to the south-east.
BE.extra: Signage switches language abruptly at the regional border: Dutch in Flanders, French in Wallonia, both in and around Brussels. Domain names end in .be.

BF.plates: White plates with black characters in a digits-letters-digits layout.
BF.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are in French, the main routes carry a white centre line with black-and-white painted kerbstones, and everything off them is unpaved red laterite.
BF.poles: Concrete poles in the cities and plain wooden poles along rural roads, often carrying just a single low-voltage line.
BF.built: Mud-brick banco walls with flat roofs in the villages, concrete block and corrugated iron in the towns, and wide dusty boulevards lined with low workshops in Ouagadougou.
BF.nature: Orange-red laterite dust over flat Sahelian savanna, scattered shea, baobab and acacia, and increasingly bare sandy ground towards the north.
BF.extra: Small motorcycles and scooters vastly outnumber cars, and roadside stalls sit under simple thatch or millet-stalk shades.

BG.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and BG; the registration uses only letters common to both alphabets, typically one or two letters, four digits and two letters.
BG.roads: White markings that are often badly worn, with wide unsealed shoulders on rural roads and a lot of patched tarmac. Kerbs and the bases of roadside trees are frequently painted white.
BG.poles: Grey concrete poles, many of them square-section with a row of holes, carry most rural distribution; older wooden poles with porcelain insulators survive in villages.
BG.built: Prefabricated panel blocks with long rows of enclosed balconies in the towns; villages have rendered or whitewashed single-storey houses with red pantiles and vine-shaded courtyards. National Revival houses have a jettied upper floor over a stone base.
BG.nature: Sunflower and rose fields on the plains, oak and beech on the Balkan range, dark conifers in the Rhodopes, and dry brown soil in the south-east.
BG.extra: All signage is Cyrillic, usually with Latin transliteration beneath on main roads. Аптека (pharmacy) and Магазин shopfronts are ubiquitous and domains end in .bg.

BH.plates: White plates with black characters, the country name in Arabic and English across the top and a short digit sequence below. Front and rear plates match.
BH.roads: Drives on the right. Wide multi-lane roads with green and blue direction signs carrying Arabic above English, yellow centre lines in places and many roundabouts.
BH.built: Low beige and white rendered villas with flat roofs, roof-mounted water tanks and high boundary walls, with glass towers clustered in Manama.
BH.nature: Flat pale limestone and sand with essentially no wild vegetation; date palms and irrigated shrubs are planted along verges and in central reservations.
BH.extra: Very short distances between everything, heavy white Toyota and Nissan traffic, and frequent sand drift along the road edge.

BI.roads: Drives on the right. Signage is in French, the tarmac is narrow with steep hairpin climbs, and markings are faded or absent outside Bujumbura.
BI.built: Mud-walled and fired-brick houses with corrugated iron roofs packed onto steep terraced hillsides, with faded colonial-era buildings in central Bujumbura.
BI.nature: Intensely green, steeply terraced hills covered in banana groves and eucalyptus stands over red-brown soil, dropping to Lake Tanganyika in the west.
BI.extra: Roads are crowded with pedestrians and with bicycles loaded far beyond their size with bananas, charcoal and sacks.

BJ.plates: White plates with black characters, the registration ending in the letters RB for Republique du Benin.
BJ.roads: Drives on the right. French-language signage, a white centre line on the main north-south corridor with black-and-white painted kerbs, speed humps in every village, and unmarked laterite side roads.
BJ.poles: Wooden poles through most of the countryside and slim concrete poles with a visible casting seam in the towns.
BJ.built: Single-storey concrete block houses with corrugated iron roofs in the south, mud-brick with thatch in the north, and stilt villages standing in the water on Lake Nokoue.
BJ.nature: Red-orange laterite dust coating roadside vegetation, oil palm and coconut near the coast, and open savanna with shea and baobab further north.
BJ.extra: Yellow-shirted zemidjan motorcycle taxis dominate every street, and smuggled Nigerian petrol is sold from racks of glass demijohns at the roadside.

BL.plates: French-style white plates with black characters.
BL.roads: Drives on the right. Roads are extremely steep and narrow with sharp hairpins and concrete or asphalt surfacing, suited to very small cars, and one road runs over the hill immediately beside the short St Jean airstrip.
BL.poles: Wooden and concrete poles on the hills, with cabling buried in central Gustavia.
BL.built: Neat, well-maintained houses with white walls, green or red shingle roofs and louvred shutters, plus Swedish-era stone buildings and a yacht-filled harbour in Gustavia.
BL.nature: Dry, steep scrubby hills with cactus, frangipani and sea grape, and small white beaches between rocky headlands.
BL.extra: Euro prices and French signage in a conspicuously wealthy, tidy setting with luxury boutiques, superyachts and open Mini Moke style beach cars.

BM.plates: Small plates with short registrations and the name Bermuda; they are noticeably smaller than European or American plates.
BM.roads: Drives on the left with an island-wide 35 kilometres per hour limit, so there are no motorways and no fast roads at all. Narrow winding lanes run between limestone walls and dense hedges, with enormous numbers of scooters.
BM.poles: Wooden poles carrying many wires, with vegetation cut back hard around them.
BM.built: Unmistakable pastel-painted limestone houses with stepped, brilliant white limewashed roofs built to harvest rainwater, plus small white buttery outbuildings with pyramid roofs.
BM.nature: Casuarina, cedar, oleander hedges and palmettos; subtropical rather than tropical, with pink-tinged sand and low rolling terrain.
BM.extra: Pink and blue buses, British-style pillar boxes and moongate stone arches in gardens. Historically no rental cars, so traffic is private vehicles and scooters only.

BN.plates: Black plates with white characters, usually a short all-numeric sequence with no state or district code. Front and rear are the same.
BN.roads: Drives on the left. Well-surfaced roads with crisp markings, green direction signs on the highway and blue on local roads, with Jawi Arabic script often set alongside or above the Latin place names.
BN.poles: Concrete poles on rural roads; much of the urban network has cabling underground or on low steel columns.
BN.built: Modern low-rise rendered buildings with metal roofs, gold-domed mosques with tall minarets, and stilted timber houses on the water at Kampong Ayer.
BN.nature: Dense lowland rainforest and secondary jungle right up to the road, with oil palm, nipa and mangrove along rivers.
BN.extra: Jawi script on street signs is the clearest separator from neighbouring Malaysia. Traffic is light, with many large Japanese SUVs and pickups and almost no motorbikes by regional standards.

BO.plates: White plates with black characters and a blue band across the top reading BOLIVIA with the flag colours.
BO.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Sealed roads carry yellow centre lines and white edges, but a large share of the network is dirt or cobble; painted black-and-white kerbs, speed bumps and toll barriers are frequent.
BO.poles: Slim round or square concrete poles dominate the Altiplano and the cities, with wooden poles more common in the eastern lowlands.
BO.built: Unrendered red brick houses with corrugated metal roofs, often unfinished with rebar standing proud; adobe walls and tin roofs in the countryside, and highland towns built tight around a central plaza.
BO.nature: Treeless brown Altiplano grassland at altitude with snow peaks on the horizon, lines of eucalyptus in the valleys, dry thorn scrub in the Chaco, and dense green forest towards the Amazon.
BO.extra: Spanish signage mixed with Aymara and Quechua place names, Estado Plurinacional wording on official signs, crowded minibuses and trufis, and women in bowler hats and pollera skirts in the highlands.

BQ.plates: Plates carry the individual island name, Bonaire, Sint Eustatius or Saba, rather than a national code.
BQ.roads: Drives on the right. Bonaire is flat with straight sealed roads and Dutch-style signs and markings, while Saba has one famously steep road with tight hairpins and concrete surfacing cut into a volcanic cone.
BQ.poles: Wooden and concrete poles on Bonaire; Saba and Sint Eustatius have short runs of poles beside the single road.
BQ.built: Bonaire has low Dutch-Caribbean houses in ochre, white and terracotta with shallow roofs, while Saba is strikingly uniform with white cottages, green shutters and red roofs enforced by building rules.
BQ.nature: Bonaire is desert with columnar cactus, divi-divi and pink salt pans holding flamingos; Saba is a green, cloud-wrapped forested cone with tree ferns.
BQ.extra: Dutch appears on official signage with Papiamento on Bonaire and English on Saba and Sint Eustatius, yet prices are in US dollars.

BR.plates: Mercosur plates: white with a blue strip across the top reading BRASIL. Older plates are grey with the city and state along the bottom.
BR.roads: Yellow centre lines and white edge lines, and traffic drives on the right. Kerbs are often painted, and roads are frequently lined with distinctive angular concrete guardrail posts.
BR.poles: Round concrete poles with a hollow, slightly tapering profile are near-universal, usually with a spiral seam visible.
BR.built: Unrendered red brick or breeze-block houses with flat concrete roofs and rebar left sticking up for a future storey.
BR.nature: Red or orange soil in the south-east, dense tropical growth, roadside banana and mango, eucalyptus plantations.
BR.extra: The Google car in Brazil often shows a long roof-mounted antenna. Portuguese signage and .br domains on shopfronts settle it against Spanish-speaking neighbours.

BS.plates: White plates with black characters, BAHAMAS across the top and the island or district of registration along the bottom.
BS.roads: Traffic drives on the left, but most cars are left-hand-drive American imports, so the driver sits on the kerb side. Roads are flat with white edge lines, low kerbs, and roundabouts on the main New Providence routes; markings are sparse on the Family Islands.
BS.poles: Wooden utility poles carrying thick bundles of cable line most streets.
BS.built: Single-storey concrete houses painted pastel pink, yellow and turquoise with hipped shingle or metal roofs, louvred windows and hurricane shutters, plus American-style strip malls and gated subdivisions around Nassau.
BS.nature: Flat white limestone ground with thin soil, Caribbean pine forest on Grand Bahama and Abaco, low coppice scrub, casuarina and coconut palms, and turquoise shallows visible from most coastal roads.
BS.extra: English signage and heavy American retail and fast-food branding; US dollars circulate alongside the pegged Bahamian dollar.

BT.plates: White plates with black Latin lettering, with codes such as BP for private vehicles and a district number; government vehicles use red plates with white lettering.
BT.roads: Drives on the left. Narrow single or one-and-a-half lane mountain roads cut into steep slopes, usually with no guardrail but with low whitewashed stone kerb blocks and painted milestones.
BT.poles: Slim timber or concrete poles carrying a small number of thin wires, following the road along the valley side.
BT.built: A mandated national style: whitewashed rammed-earth or masonry walls, timber-framed bay windows with trefoil arches and painted decoration, and shallow pitched shingle or corrugated roofs set slightly above the walls.
BT.nature: Extremely steep forested Himalayan valleys with blue pine, oak, rhododendron and hanging moss, cut by fast grey-green rivers.
BT.extra: Strings of prayer flags on ridges and bridges, whitewashed chortens beside the road, and painted wooden bridges. Traffic is very light and mostly Indian-built cars and trucks.

BV.extra: An uninhabited, almost entirely glaciated volcanic island in the South Atlantic with no roads, buildings or vehicles and no street-level imagery of any kind.

BW.plates: White reflective plates with black characters, typically the letter B followed by three digits and three letters.
BW.roads: Drives on the left. Long straight tarmac with a white centre line and yellow edge lines, low white-painted marker posts, and frequent triangular warning signs for elephants, donkeys and cattle.
BW.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms on rural roads, slim concrete poles in the towns, and tall steel lattice pylons along the main corridors.
BW.built: Low flat-roofed or shallow-pitched buildings in beige and ochre render, tin-roofed rondavels in the villages, and wide single-storey shopping strips with deep shaded verandas.
BW.nature: Pale grey-white Kalahari sand, thorny acacia and mopane scrub, flat horizons with almost no relief, and dry grass that bleaches to straw colour.
BW.extra: Cattle, donkeys and goats loose on the tarmac are near-guaranteed, and Choppies and Spar signage appears in almost every town.

BY.plates: White plate with black characters and, unusually, the country marking on the right: a small panel with the red-and-green flag above the letters BY. Format is four digits, two letters, then a single region digit.
BY.roads: Wide, very straight and conspicuously well-kept roads with crisp white markings and closely mown verges. Main-route direction signs are green and local ones blue, following the Soviet standard.
BY.poles: Grey concrete poles dominate, either square-section with holes or round and tapered; villages often use shorter wooden poles set on concrete stubs.
BY.built: Soviet-era panel and brick apartment blocks in the towns, and single-storey village houses of painted timber with carved window surrounds in blue, green or white under corrugated or slate roofs.
BY.nature: Flat land with extensive birch and pine forest, drained marshland, and large open fields of potatoes, rye and flax.
BY.extra: Signage mixes Belarusian and Russian, often with Latin transliteration added underneath. Official Street View coverage is very thin, so much imagery is user-contributed panoramas.

BZ.plates: White plates with black characters showing the district of registration, such as Belize, Cayo, Corozal, Orange Walk, Stann Creek or Toledo.
BZ.roads: Traffic drives on the right, which instantly separates Belize from its English-speaking Caribbean neighbours. Highways are two-lane with white edge lines and often no centre line at all, punctuated by very severe speed humps and simple roadside bus shelters.
BZ.built: Timber houses raised on wooden or concrete stilts with corrugated zinc roofs, alongside plain concrete-block buildings; villages string out along the highway with open-fronted shops.
BZ.nature: Dense tropical broadleaf forest with cohune palms, citrus and sugar cane plantations, open pine savanna with scattered Caribbean pine on poor soils, and mangrove along the coast.
BZ.extra: English is the official signage language, with Spanish and Belizean Creole alongside it. Mennonite horse-drawn buggies appear in Cayo and Orange Walk, and Belikin beer branding and .bz addresses are common.

CA.plates: Plates vary by province: Ontario white with blue lettering, Quebec white with blue lettering and Je me souviens, British Columbia blue on white, Alberta white with red. Quebec and Alberta issue a rear plate only.
CA.roads: Traffic drives on the right, with yellow lines separating opposing traffic and white lane and edge lines, matching the American pattern. Speed limits are in kilometres per hour on MAXIMUM signs, warning signs are yellow diamonds, and tall flexible snow stakes mark shoulders in the north.
CA.poles: Tall wooden poles with horizontal crossarms and barrel transformers, very close to the American arrangement.
CA.built: Timber-framed houses with vinyl or clapboard siding, asphalt shingle roofs and detached garages; prairie towns built around grain elevators and level crossings, and low brick main streets in the east.
CA.nature: Boreal spruce, pine and birch across the north, sugar maple and mixed hardwood in the east, grain prairie on the plains, and tall Douglas fir rainforest on the Pacific coast.
CA.extra: Bilingual French and English signage in Quebec and New Brunswick, with ARRET on Quebec stop signs. Look for .ca addresses, Tim Hortons, Canada Post kerbside boxes and provincial route shields such as Ontario's crown.

CC.plates: Australian-format plates bearing the territory name.
CC.roads: Drives on the left. A single short sealed road runs the length of West Island with almost no traffic, while Home Island has only sandy tracks used by buggies and motorbikes and most travel is by ferry.
CC.poles: Short wooden poles beside the one road.
CC.built: West Island has fibro and prefabricated Australian bungalows with metal roofs; Home Island is a Cocos Malay village of small pastel houses around a mosque.
CC.nature: Coconut palms in dense plantation rows across flat coral cays, brilliant turquoise lagoon water and blinding white sand, with no elevation at all.
CC.extra: Malay language and Islamic dress on Home Island sit alongside standard Australian road signs, which is the giveaway combination.

CD.roads: Drives on the right. Signage is in French, Kinshasa's boulevards have white markings and painted kerbs, and the overwhelming majority of the country's roads are unsurfaced red earth.
CD.poles: Concrete poles in Kinshasa and Lubumbashi, with rural roads often having no power line alongside them at all.
CD.built: Belgian colonial buildings with deep verandas in the old centres, endless single-storey breeze-block houses under rusting corrugated iron, and a cluster of glass towers in Kinshasa's Gombe district.
CD.nature: Deep red-orange laterite, dense equatorial rainforest across the north and centre, and open green miombo woodland on the Katangan plateau.
CD.extra: Bright yellow Kinshasa taxis and minibuses, and roads crowded with pedestrians and hand-pushed carts.

CF.nature: Red laterite soil under open savanna with scattered trees across most of the country, turning to dense rainforest in the south-west.

CG.roads: Drives on the right. The Brazzaville to Pointe-Noire highway is smooth new tarmac with white markings and steel barriers, while most other roads are red laterite; signage is in French.
CG.built: Concrete block houses with corrugated iron roofs, French colonial buildings with verandas in central Brazzaville, and dense low-rise districts with painted shopfronts.
CG.nature: Dense rainforest and swamp in the north, pale white-yellow sand and grass on the Bateke plateaus near Brazzaville, and red laterite cuttings.

CH.plates: White plate with black characters, no EU strip; the two-letter canton code is followed by digits, with the Swiss cross and the canton coat of arms at the right-hand end. The front plate is noticeably smaller than the wide rear plate.
CH.roads: Motorway direction signs are green and all other main roads blue, which is the reverse of most of Europe and the strongest single tell. Pedestrian crossings are painted yellow, and yellow lines mark restricted parking.
CH.poles: Overhead distribution is largely buried; rural areas keep some wooden poles and the railways add distinctive overhead catenary almost everywhere.
CH.built: Timber chalets with wide eaves, carved balconies and neatly stacked firewood in the mountains; elsewhere rendered houses with shutters, immaculate stonework and conspicuously tidy maintenance.
CH.nature: Steep close-cropped alpine pasture, dark spruce forest, grey limestone and granite peaks, and terraced vineyards dropping to deep blue lakes.
CH.extra: The language on signs changes by region between German, French, Italian and Romansh. Yellow PostBus stops, yellow post boxes and the motorway vignette sticker on the windscreen are all reliable markers; domains end in .ch.

CI.plates: White plates with black characters; newer issues carry a blue band on the left with the flag and the letters CI.
CI.roads: Drives on the right. Abidjan has genuine motorway with white markings, green direction signs and crash barriers, while the interior is two-lane tarmac with black-and-white painted kerbs and laterite side roads.
CI.poles: Square-section concrete poles in the cities and wooden poles inland.
CI.built: The Plateau district of Abidjan shows a skyline of 1970s concrete towers, while elsewhere single-storey breeze-block with corrugated iron and brightly painted shopfronts is the norm.
CI.nature: Orange-red laterite soil, vast cocoa, rubber and oil palm plantations, lagoons fringed with coconut on the coast, and open savanna in the north.
CI.extra: Abidjan's metered taxis are orange-red, and Orange and MTN paint colours cover roadside kiosks and container shops.

CK.roads: Drives on the left. Rarotonga has one sealed 32 kilometre ring road with a low speed limit and an older inner coral back road, with scooters far outnumbering cars.
CK.poles: Concrete and wooden poles following the ring road, with lines running over the roadside vegetation.
CK.built: Single-storey houses with corrugated metal roofs, whitewashed coral-limestone Cook Islands Christian Church buildings with blue trim, and family graves set in the front gardens.
CK.nature: Jagged green volcanic peaks rising steeply in the centre of Rarotonga, coconut palms and taro beds, with the lagoon only metres from the road in places.
CK.extra: New Zealand dollars and New Zealand-style road signs. Roadside stalls sell fruit on an honesty box system.

CL.plates: White plates with black characters in a four letter, two digit format, with a small blue panel on the left carrying CHILE. Older cars still run two letters and four digits.
CL.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Centre lines are generally white, with yellow used on painted kerbs and no-overtaking sections; motorways are modern, heavily tolled and well signed, and rural roads have white delineator posts and W-beam guardrail.
CL.poles: Round grey concrete poles are common in cities and the central valley, while wooden poles are widespread in the forested south.
CL.built: Rendered concrete and brick houses with corrugated metal roofs painted red or green, timber shingle-clad houses in the rainy south, and low adobe frontages with clay tiles in central valley towns.
CL.nature: Bare grey-brown desert with essentially no vegetation in the north, vineyards and poplar rows in the central valley, and southern beech, monkey puzzle, lakes and volcanoes in the south, with the Andes almost always to the east.
CL.extra: Spanish signage with distinctly Chilean wording, PARE stop signs, Copec filling stations, and prices in pesos running to thousands.

CM.plates: White plates with black characters; newer issues have a blue band on the left with the flag and the letters CAM.
CM.roads: Drives on the right. Signage is mostly French with English in the north-west and south-west, main roads have a white centre line, and rural roads are deeply rutted red earth.
CM.poles: Concrete poles in the cities and wooden poles through the countryside, with heavy cable tangles at junctions.
CM.built: Concrete block with corrugated iron in the south, steeply pitched tin roofs in the rainy western highlands, and mud-brick with conical thatch in the far north.
CM.nature: Dense green rainforest and oil palm over deep red laterite in the south, dark volcanic soil around Mount Cameroon, and dry acacia savanna in the north.
CM.extra: Bright yellow taxis fill Douala and Yaounde, and roadside markets crowd right up to the tarmac under corrugated awnings.

CN.plates: Blue plates with white characters, opening with a single Chinese character for the province and then a letter for the city; electric vehicles use longer green plates with black characters.
CN.roads: Drives on the right. Yellow centre lines separate opposing traffic and white lines separate same-direction lanes; expressway signs are green with white text and urban expressway signs are blue, with place names in Chinese above pinyin.
CN.poles: Round or square concrete poles in the countryside and galvanised steel poles in cities, with tall lattice transmission towers crossing farmland.
CN.built: Concrete frames clad in small white bathroom-style tiles, blue-green tinted glass, and rows of identical high-rise blocks on the edge of even small towns.
CN.nature: Enormously varied, from loess plateau and dry northern plains to terraced rice and subtropical broadleaf in the south, with fast-growing poplar rows along northern roads.
CN.extra: Red banners with white or yellow characters hung on walls and fences, blue or green corrugated metal hoarding around construction sites, and dense speed-camera gantries.

CO.plates: Private cars carry bright yellow plates with black characters, three letters and three digits, with the city of registration in small text. Public service vehicles use white plates and official vehicles blue, and motorcycles use the same yellow scheme.
CO.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edge lines, with mountain highways cut into steep slopes, frequent landslide netting and gabion walls, and black-and-white painted kerbs and concrete bollards in towns.
CO.poles: Round or square grey concrete poles are the norm, often with a visible casting seam; wooden poles are rare.
CO.built: Exposed red clay brick is everywhere, on houses and apartment blocks alike. In the coffee region look for whitewashed bahareque houses with brightly painted doors, timber balconies and clay tile roofs.
CO.nature: Intensely green steep Andean slopes with coffee, plantain and tall wax palms, tropical lowland forest in the Amazon and Choco, and dry cactus scrub on the Guajira peninsula.
CO.extra: Motorcyclists must display their plate number on a reflective vest and on the helmet, which is an immediate Colombian giveaway. Spanish signage, .co addresses, and roadside arepa and tinto stalls.

CR.plates: White plates with black characters, three letters and three digits, with a blue band across the top reading COSTA RICA beside the flag.
CR.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edges, on narrow two-lane roads with deep open concrete drainage channels at the verge; one-lane bridges signed CEDA are common in the countryside.
CR.poles: Square-section reinforced concrete poles with chamfered corners are very common, alongside round concrete and some wooden poles.
CR.built: Single-storey houses in painted concrete block or rendered masonry with corrugated metal roofs, barred windows and carports; town centres have low arcaded shopfronts around a park and church.
CR.nature: Exceptionally lush, with coffee terraces, banana and oil palm plantations, cloud forest on the volcanic spine, and roadside heliconia, bamboo and cecropia.
CR.extra: Spanish signage, Pura Vida branding, ICE utility markings on poles and cabinets, .cr addresses and a very high proportion of pickup trucks.

CU.plates: White plates with black characters, with the leading letter coding ownership, such as private, state or rental. Older colour-coded plates in yellow, blue or orange still turn up on some vehicles.
CU.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Road markings are faded or absent on many routes, junctions carry simple blue-and-white signs, and the Autopista Nacional is a wide, almost empty dual carriageway with grass verges and few markings.
CU.poles: Square and round concrete poles are standard, most of them visibly old and weathered grey.
CU.built: Spanish colonial streets with arcaded pavements, tall shuttered windows and peeling pastel render, plus Soviet-era concrete apartment blocks on the edges of towns.
CU.nature: Rolling green farmland with royal palms standing singly in open fields, sugar cane, tobacco in the west, and steep limestone mogotes around Vinales.
CU.extra: 1950s American cars and Ladas, horse-drawn carts, and state political billboards in place of commercial advertising. The near-total absence of brand signage is itself the tell.

CV.plates: White plates with black characters in a Portuguese-style grouped layout, with a blue band on the left on newer issues.
CV.roads: Drives on the right. Many older roads are hand-laid basalt cobblestone, modern tarmac carries white markings, and cliff roads have low white-painted stone parapets rather than steel barriers.
CV.poles: Slim concrete poles carrying lines along steep volcanic slopes.
CV.built: Flat-roofed concrete and stone houses painted in pastel pinks, blues and yellows, frequently with an unfinished upper floor and rebar, clustered tightly on steep ground.
CV.nature: Bare brown and black volcanic rock, dry terraced valleys with sugar cane and banana on the greener islands, and pale sand dunes on Sal and Boa Vista.
CV.extra: Aluguer shared Hiace minibuses work the switchback roads, and the sea is visible from almost every viewpoint.

CW.plates: White plates with black characters carrying the word Curacao.
CW.roads: Drives on the right. Dutch-style signage, markings and roundabouts, with a genuinely motorway-standard ring road around Willemstad.
CW.poles: Concrete poles along main roads, with lighting columns of Dutch pattern in the urban area.
CW.built: Willemstad's Dutch merchant houses with curved gables painted in vivid pastels along the harbour are unmistakable; inland there are low concrete houses and ochre-and-white landhuizen plantation houses.
CW.nature: Arid thorn scrub with columnar cactus and divi-divi, low flat-topped hills, and no rivers or dense greenery.
CW.extra: Dutch and Papiamento appear together on signage. The Queen Emma floating pontoon bridge and the large oil refinery behind Willemstad are strong landmarks.

CX.roads: Drives on the left with Australian signage. Narrow sealed roads wind through dense jungle, and in the migration season they are partly closed with temporary barriers, crab bridges and grids to protect the red crabs.
CX.poles: Wooden poles along the settled roads, with long dark unlit stretches between.
CX.built: Prefabricated Australian-style housing and worker accommodation, plus Chinese temples, a mosque and Malay kampong buildings in the settlement, with the phosphate mine and cantilever loader dominating the port.
CX.nature: Dense rainforest on stepped limestone terraces with huge buttressed trees, sheer coastal cliffs, and red crabs crossing the road in vast numbers in season.
CX.extra: Australian English signage appears alongside Chinese and Malay text, an unusual combination on Australian-standard roads.

CY.plates: White front plate and yellow rear plate with black characters, a blue EU strip and CY. Three letters followed by three or four digits.
CY.roads: Traffic drives on the left and road furniture follows British patterns, including double yellow lines at the kerb and give-way markings. Direction signs are bilingual, with Greek above the Latin transliteration.
CY.poles: Concrete poles with a squared profile are common, alongside older wooden poles; overhead cabling is heavy in villages.
CY.built: Flat-roofed concrete houses in sandy ochre or white render, almost all carrying a solar water heater panel with a horizontal white or grey cylinder on the roof. Arched verandas and deep window reveals are typical.
CY.nature: Dry scrub with carob and olive trees, terraced hillsides, Aleppo pine in the Troodos highlands, and dusty red-brown soil.
CY.extra: The rooftop solar cylinders are the single quickest tell. Road names use Leoforos and Odos, and post boxes are British in shape but painted yellow.

CZ.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and CZ; format is a digit, two letters, a space, then four digits. Front and rear are the same.
CZ.roads: Motorway direction signs are green and other main roads blue. Markings are white, roadside delineator posts are white with a black cap, and rural roads are frequently lined with regular avenues of fruit or lime trees.
CZ.poles: Grey concrete poles are typical, often a slim tapered post with a wider braced or latticed section near the base in rural areas.
CZ.built: Villages of rendered houses in pale yellow, pink and green with steep red tile roofs and the gable facing the road. Towns add baroque churches with onion-domed towers and large panelák housing estates on the outskirts.
CZ.nature: Rolling arable land with spruce and pine plantations, hop fields on tall wire frames in Bohemia, and pale sandstone rock towers in the north.
CZ.extra: Houses commonly carry two number plaques side by side, a red one and a blue one. Czech uses ř, ě and ů, and domains end in .cz.

DE.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and D, then a one-to-three letter district code, two small round stickers stacked together, then letters and digits. The pair of round seals in the middle is the clearest sign.
DE.roads: Motorway signs are blue and Bundesstraße direction signs are yellow with black text, which is a strong tell. Markings are white, and the roadside delineator posts are white with a black band and a rectangular reflector.
DE.poles: Overhead lines are largely absent in towns; rural areas use plain wooden poles and occasional concrete posts, with lattice steel pylons for transmission.
DE.built: Rendered houses with external roller-shutter boxes above the windows and steep red or dark grey tiled roofs, often heavily covered in solar panels. Older centres show black-and-white half-timbering with carved beams.
DE.nature: Neatly managed spruce and beech forest planted in rows, tidy rolling farmland, and large numbers of white wind turbines on the northern plains.
DE.extra: Town boundaries are marked by yellow rectangular signs with the place name in black. Street name plates are usually white with black text or blue enamel, and domains end in .de.

DJ.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are in French and Arabic, the Ethiopia corridor is well-surfaced tarmac across bare desert, and lesser roads have no markings at all.
DJ.built: Low flat-roofed concrete buildings in white, cream and pale blue, French colonial arcades and shuttered facades in Djibouti City, and corrugated iron in the outer districts.
DJ.nature: Almost treeless black volcanic rock and pale salt flats, scattered thorny acacia and doum palms, and heavy heat shimmer over stony desert.
DJ.extra: Endless convoys of container lorries running to and from Ethiopia are the defining traffic on the main highway.

DK.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and DK and, most distinctively, a thin red border line running right around the edge of the plate. Format is two letters and five digits.
DK.roads: White markings with clear edge lines, and a separate raised or kerbed cycle track alongside almost every urban and many rural roads. Delineator posts are white with reflectors, and speed limits are shown in round red-ringed signs.
DK.poles: Most distribution cable is buried, so overhead lines are scarce; surviving rural poles are plain creosoted wood.
DK.built: Red or pale yellow brick houses with red pantile roofs and white-painted window frames, plus thatched cottages in the countryside. Village churches are whitewashed with stepped gables and red roofs.
DK.nature: Very flat and wind-exposed, with wheat and bright yellow rapeseed fields, dense conifer windbreak hedges, beech woodland, and sandy dune coasts with marram grass.
DK.extra: Private gardens very often have a tall white flagpole. Danish uses æ, ø and å, street names end in -vej and -gade, and wind turbines are visible almost everywhere.

DM.plates: White plates with black characters and a leading letter marking the vehicle class.
DM.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Roads are narrow, steep and twisting with almost no markings, concrete drainage channels along the uphill side, and short concrete-paved sections on the steepest gradients.
DM.poles: Wooden utility poles carrying a few lines, often planted into steep banks right at the road edge.
DM.built: Small concrete or timber houses with corrugated metal roofs clinging to steep ground, painted in strong colours, reached by steps up from the road behind retaining walls.
DM.nature: Exceptionally dense mountain rainforest with tree ferns, bananas and coconut, deep river gorges and black volcanic sand beaches; almost no flat ground anywhere.
DM.extra: English signage with French Creole place names such as Soufriere and Pointe Michel, right-hand-drive Japanese imports, and East Caribbean dollar prices.

DO.plates: White plates with black characters and a coloured header reading REPUBLICA DOMINICANA; private cars use an A prefix followed by six digits.
DO.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edges on main routes, with heavy speed bumps in every village and black-and-white paint on kerbs and tree trunks.
DO.poles: Round and octagonal concrete poles dominate, carrying dense, visibly tangled low-voltage wiring.
DO.built: Painted concrete block houses with flat roofs and rebar left for a future floor, zinc-roofed timber houses in the countryside, and shopfronts covered edge to edge in beer and lottery advertising.
DO.nature: Royal palms over sugar cane and pasture, densely green mountains in the Cordillera Central, and a dry south-west with cactus and thorn scrub.
DO.extra: Spanish signage; banca lottery and sports-betting kiosks and colmado corner shops appear on almost every block, motoconcho motorcycle taxis are everywhere, and Presidente beer branding is ubiquitous.

DZ.plates: White plates with black characters, all numeric, the last two digits giving the wilaya (province) code. Many older cars still carry a yellow rear plate in the inherited French style.
DZ.roads: Drives on the right. Direction signs are bilingual with Arabic above French, motorway panels are green, and kerbstones and tree trunks are frequently painted white or black and white.
DZ.poles: Slim round concrete poles through towns and villages, with steel lattice pylons carrying the transmission lines across open country.
DZ.built: Unfinished concrete-frame houses with red hollow-brick infill and rebar left standing on flat roofs, cream and sand render, and French colonial arcades in the older town centres.
DZ.nature: A narrow coastal belt of Aleppo pine, eucalyptus, olive and prickly pear over reddish-brown soil, turning to pale stony grey ground and then sand south of the Atlas.
DZ.extra: Traffic is dominated by small Renault and Peugeot saloons, and in Kabylie official signs carry Tifinagh alongside Arabic and French.

EC.plates: White plates with black characters, three letters and three or four digits, with ECUADOR and the province of registration printed across the top.
EC.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edges on generally well-surfaced two-lane highways, with concrete barriers on mountain sections, frequent painted speed bumps and toll plazas.
EC.poles: Round and square concrete poles are the norm in towns and along highways; wooden poles are unusual.
EC.built: Unrendered red brick or concrete block with flat roofs and protruding rebar, corrugated zinc roofs in the coastal lowlands, and low colonial arcades with clay tiles in Andean towns.
EC.nature: Steep, intensely green Andean slopes with patchwork fields and eucalyptus, treeless paramo grassland at height, banana and cacao plantations on the coastal plain, and rainforest in the Oriente.
EC.extra: Spanish signage with Quichua place names, and prices in US dollars, which separates Ecuador from Colombia and Peru. Large painted provincial government works signs are common on the roadside.

EE.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and EST, black characters, formatted as three digits then three letters.
EE.roads: A high proportion of rural roads are unsealed gravel with a pale grey surface and deep drainage ditches on both sides. Markings on paved roads are white, warning triangles have a white background, and tall reflective snow stakes line many verges.
EE.poles: Untreated grey wooden poles are the standard, often noticeably weathered and sometimes leaning, with simple single crossarms.
EE.built: Timber houses clad in horizontal or vertical boards, painted dark red, yellow or left bare, alongside Soviet-era brick and panel blocks. Northern towns show pale limestone walls and plain Lutheran church towers.
EE.nature: Flat land under dense pine, spruce and birch forest, with raised bogs, juniper scrub on thin limestone soils, and scattered granite erratic boulders.
EE.extra: Estonian piles up vowels and uses õ, ä, ö and ü; look for words like tee, tänav and küla. Domains end in .ee and settlement density is very low.

EG.plates: White plates with a blue band across the top reading Egypt in Arabic and Latin, and both Arabic and Latin characters below. Private cars use blue characters, taxis orange and commercial vehicles red.
EG.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are bilingual Arabic and English, green on motorways and blue in urban areas, and kerbs, central barriers and tree trunks are painted in black-and-white or red-and-white stripes.
EG.poles: Concrete poles both round and square, with steel lattice towers marching alongside the desert highways and canal roads.
EG.built: Unfinished red-brick apartment blocks on exposed concrete frames with rebar, flat roofs stacked with satellite dishes and water tanks, and dusty beige render on everything.
EG.nature: Bare tan desert beginning abruptly at the edge of the irrigated land, with intensely green date palms, sugar cane and fields lining the Nile and its canals.
EG.extra: White-and-black Cairo taxis, tuk-tuks in the delta towns, and painted speed humps at the entrance to every village.

EH.plates: Moroccan-style plates: white with black characters, Arabic numerals and an Arabic letter, with a regional number at the right, and no EU or country strip.
EH.roads: Drives on the right. A single well-surfaced two-lane national road runs down the coast in long empty straights with sand drifting across the tarmac, and there are frequent military and gendarmerie checkpoints.
EH.poles: Concrete poles along the coast road, with large wind farms of white turbines near Laayoune and Boujdour.
EH.built: Low flat-roofed concrete buildings in sand and ochre tones, new Moroccan administrative blocks, schools and mosques in Laayoune and Dakhla, and nomad tents on the desert margins.
EH.nature: Flat stony hamada desert and sand sheets with almost no vegetation, and a grey Atlantic fog belt with surf along the western edge.
EH.extra: Bilingual Arabic and French signage in Moroccan style, Moroccan flags and police, and a diffuse grey coastal light very different from the inland Sahara.

ER.built: Asmara is full of Italian modernist and art deco buildings in pale render with curved balconies and streamlined facades, an unmistakable look; elsewhere flat-roofed stone and mud houses dominate.
ER.nature: Bare rocky highland escarpment with terraced fields and prickly pear over red-brown soil, dropping steeply to hot pale sandy coastal desert.

ES.plates: White plate front and rear with black characters, four digits followed by three consonants, and a blue EU strip with E. No province marking on modern plates.
ES.roads: Motorway and dual carriageway signs are blue while national road shields are red with white numbers. Markings are white, kerbs are painted yellow where parking is banned, and roadside marker posts are white with a red reflective face.
ES.poles: Concrete poles, both round tapered and square-section, are standard in the countryside, with steel lattice pylons crossing open plains.
ES.built: Whitewashed pueblos with flat or shallow pantile roofs and wrought-iron window grilles in the south, brick and render apartment blocks with glazed enclosed balconies in the cities, and grey stone with slate roofs in the wetter north.
ES.nature: Dry ochre and deep red soils, olive groves planted in vast regular grids, holm oak dehesa grazing, Aleppo pine, arid scrub on the meseta, and green eucalyptus-planted hills along the Atlantic coast.
ES.extra: Large black silhouette bulls on hilltops beside main roads are a well-known Spanish marker. Signage is bilingual with Catalan, Basque or Galician in those regions, street names appear on white ceramic tiles, and domains end in .es.

ET.plates: Plates carry Amharic script alongside Latin characters, with a small side panel giving the regional code number. Colour indicates vehicle class, with private cars most often on blue.
ET.roads: Drives on the right. New Chinese-built expressways have crisp white markings and steel guardrails, but most roads are two-lane with faded lines, and warning signs show Amharic above English.
ET.poles: Slim round concrete poles along the newer roads, with wooden poles and simple timber A-frames in rural areas.
ET.built: Round tukul huts with conical thatch or corrugated iron in the countryside, stone and wattle walls, and Addis Ababa condominium blocks in orange, cream and blue render wrapped in eucalyptus-pole scaffolding.
ET.nature: Red-brown to near-black volcanic soil, eucalyptus plantations lining almost every road, flat-topped acacia and candelabra euphorbia, and high green plateau cut by deep gorges.
ET.extra: Blue-and-white minibus taxis and old Ladas, livestock and donkeys sharing the tarmac, and people walking the verges in white cotton shawls.

FI.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and FIN and a thin black border line around the edge. Format is three letters, a hyphen, then three digits.
FI.roads: Warning triangles have a yellow background rather than white. Markings are white with a dashed edge line, and roadsides carry tall snow stakes and frequent elk warning signs; verges are usually cut back to a wide grass strip with a ditch.
FI.poles: Tall creosoted wooden poles, often in pairs or with long crossarms, run along forest roads and field edges.
FI.built: Timber houses painted red-ochre, yellow or grey with white window trim and steep standing-seam metal roofs. Towns have low, light-rendered apartment blocks in pale grey and white among the trees.
FI.nature: Continuous boreal spruce, pine and birch forest, huge numbers of lakes, low granite outcrops and gently rolling or flat terrain.
FI.extra: Finnish words are long and double letters abound; coastal and southern areas add a Swedish name underneath on signs. Domains end in .fi and road numbers appear in plain rectangles.

FJ.plates: White plates with black characters. Taxis carry distinctive yellow plates and are very numerous on the main roads.
FJ.roads: Drives on the left. The Queens Road and Kings Road ring Viti Levu as a two-lane sealed route with patchy white edge lines and frequent narrow bridges, while side roads turn to orange-brown gravel and mud.
FJ.poles: Concrete poles along the main highways and weathered wooden poles inland, usually carrying a low, untidy bundle of lines.
FJ.built: Single-storey houses in painted concrete block or timber with corrugated-iron roofs, often raised slightly on blocks, plus tin-roofed village halls and roadside produce stalls.
FJ.nature: Sugar cane fields across the drier western side, coconut palms, huge spreading raintrees shading the road, and steep green volcanic ridges inland.
FJ.extra: Hindu temples with brightly painted gopuram towers, mosques and Methodist churches appear in the same few kilometres, reflecting the Indo-Fijian and iTaukei mix. Speed limits are in kilometres per hour.

FK.plates: UK-style plates, white at the front and yellow at the rear, with short registrations beginning with the letter F.
FK.roads: Drives on the left. Outside Stanley almost every route is a single-track gravel road with passing places, no markings and cattle grids, with the Stanley to Mount Pleasant road the main artery.
FK.poles: Very few poles; wooden poles with overhead lines in Stanley itself and wind turbines on the ridges nearby.
FK.built: Stanley has brightly painted corrugated-iron clad houses with white window frames and a stone cathedral with a whalebone arch; the camp has isolated clusters of tin-roofed farm buildings.
FK.nature: Completely treeless. Pale white grass, low diddle-dee heath, peat cuttings, and long grey stone runs of frost-shattered boulders spilling down the slopes.
FK.extra: Red British pillar boxes and phone boxes in Stanley, Land Rovers and pickups everywhere, and yellow minefield warning signs on fenced ground near the coast.

FM.plates: US-sized plates issued separately by each of the four states, so the plate carries a state name such as Pohnpei, Chuuk, Yap or Kosrae.
FM.roads: Drives on the right. Pohnpei's circumferential road alternates between patched asphalt and rough coral gravel, with dense jungle rising immediately inland and no lane markings over long stretches.
FM.poles: Concrete and wooden poles, often with vegetation growing up them in the constant humidity.
FM.built: Concrete-block single-storey buildings with rusting corrugated roofs, small churches, and grey Japanese-era concrete ruins standing overgrown beside the road on Pohnpei and Chuuk.
FM.nature: Extremely wet, dark green rainforest running right down to the road edge, mangroves along the shore, betel nut palms and frequent low cloud on the peaks.
FM.extra: On Yap, large carved stone money discs stand in rows beside village paths. Red betel-nut spit stains on the roadside are common.

FO.plates: White plates with black characters, two letters then three digits, with a blue side strip carrying the Faroese flag and the code FO.
FO.roads: Drives on the right. Immaculate narrow asphalt with white edge lines, an unusual density of tunnels including long single-lane ones with passing bays and rough rock walls, and sheep standing on the carriageway.
FO.poles: Very few poles because most cabling is buried; what you see instead are lighting columns, tunnel portals and avalanche shelters.
FO.built: Small timber houses clad in black tar or painted red, ochre and white with white window frames, many with living turf roofs, clustered tightly around a small harbour.
FO.nature: Absolutely treeless. Steep green basalt terraces stepping up from the sea, thin waterfalls down every cliff, low cloud and constant sheep.
FO.extra: Danish-pattern road signs with Faroese place names. There is a roundabout inside a subsea tunnel at the Eysturoy junction, lit in blue.

FR.plates: White plate front and rear with black characters in an AB-123-CD pattern, a blue EU strip with F on the left and a second narrow blue band on the right showing a regional logo above the two-digit department number.
FR.roads: Motorway direction signs are blue, routes towards major destinations are signed in green, and local signs are white. Roadside delineator posts are white with a red reflective band, and many rural roads are lined with regularly spaced plane trees.
FR.poles: Rural distribution uses plain concrete posts and wooden poles; in villages the low-voltage cable is frequently bracketed directly onto house walls.
FR.built: Pale limestone or cream-rendered houses with wooden shutters in grey, blue or dark green. Grey slate roofs in the north and west, orange roman pantiles in the south, and a Mairie with a tricolour in almost every village.
FR.nature: Highly varied: plane and poplar avenues, vineyards in neat rows, huge wheat and sunflower fields, and dry aromatic garrigue with holm oak in the Mediterranean south.
FR.extra: Village entry signs are white rectangles with a red border and the place name in black. Street plaques are blue with a white border, and boulangerie, tabac and pharmacie signs are everywhere.

GA.roads: Drives on the right. Signage is in French, Libreville's main roads have white markings and painted kerbs, and long stretches inland are red laterite.
GA.built: Concrete block buildings with corrugated iron roofs, French-influenced administrative buildings in Libreville, and small towns where rusting tin roofs are almost swallowed by the forest.
GA.nature: Dense equatorial rainforest pressing right up to the road edge, deep red-orange laterite cuttings, and oil palm plantations.

GB.plates: White front plate and yellow rear plate with black characters, typically two letters, two digits, a space and three letters, with a blue strip reading UK on the left.
GB.roads: Traffic drives on the left and distances are in miles. Single and double yellow lines run along the kerb to mark parking restrictions, motorway signs are blue, primary route signs green with yellow route numbers, and local signs white with black text.
GB.poles: Slim creosoted wooden poles, often with a single crossarm and a slight lean, carry rural distribution.
GB.built: Long terraces of red brick houses with chimney stacks, bay windows and small front walls; pebbledash and render in suburbia, slate roofs in the north and Wales, and honey or grey stone cottages in rural areas.
GB.nature: Green fields hemmed by thick hedgerows and dry stone walls, mature oak and ash in field corners, rolling chalk downs, and brown heather moorland at altitude.
GB.extra: Roundabouts are everywhere and road words such as SLOW and KEEP CLEAR are painted on the carriageway. Red post boxes, Welsh bilingual signs in Wales and Gaelic ones in parts of Scotland, and .co.uk domains on shopfronts all confirm it.

GD.plates: White plates with black characters and a leading letter marking the vehicle class.
GD.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Roads are narrow, steep and winding with little or no centre marking, deep roadside concrete drains, and sharp blind bends through villages.
GD.poles: Wooden utility poles carrying a small number of lines.
GD.built: Small concrete houses with corrugated metal or hipped roofs painted in strong colours, terraced into hillsides, with occasional older timber houses and stone estate walls.
GD.nature: Steep green volcanic hills under rainforest, nutmeg and cocoa grown beneath shade trees, bananas and breadfruit, and a drier scrubbier south-west.
GD.extra: English signage, East Caribbean dollar prices and right-hand-drive Japanese used cars.

GE.plates: White plates with black characters and a blue band on the left showing GE and the flag. Format is two letters, three digits, two letters.
GE.roads: Drives on the right. Green signs on the main east-west route and blue elsewhere, with Georgian above Latin, and a mixture of new smooth asphalt and badly broken rural surfaces.
GE.poles: Grey concrete poles, round or square, frequently leaning, with older wooden poles surviving on village lanes.
GE.built: Soviet-era concrete blocks with irregular self-built balcony extensions, plus older houses with deep carved timber verandas and rusting corrugated roofs.
GE.nature: Green and wet in the west with vines, tea and subtropical growth, drier grassy hills in the east, and high snow-covered Caucasus ridges to the north.
GE.extra: Huge numbers of imported second-hand Toyota Priuses and white Mitsubishi Delica vans, many of them right-hand drive despite right-hand traffic. Roadside stalls sell churchkhela strings.

GF.plates: French plates: white with black characters, a blue EU strip with F on the left, and a right-hand band showing the department number 973 with the local logo.
GF.roads: Drives on the right. Full French road furniture with white markings, European give-way and speed signs and roundabouts, concentrated on the single coastal RN1 and RN2; everything inland is forest track.
GF.poles: Concrete poles along the coastal road, with the forest cut back in a narrow corridor.
GF.built: French administrative buildings and supermarkets, Creole timber houses with shutters and verandahs in Cayenne, and stilted Maroon and Amerindian villages along the rivers.
GF.nature: Unbroken Amazonian rainforest right up to the road edge, bright red laterite soil in cuttings, mangrove-lined coast and brown sediment-laden sea.
GF.extra: Euro prices, gendarmerie and French-language signage in South America. The Kourou space centre with its launch complexes is visible from the coastal road.

GG.plates: Purely numeric registrations with no letters at all, on UK-style white front and yellow rear plates, which separates Guernsey from Jersey and the Isle of Man immediately.
GG.roads: Drives on the left with a 35 miles per hour island maximum. Very narrow granite-walled lanes, yellow filter-in-turn arrows painted at junctions, yellow stop lines instead of white, and Ruettes Tranquilles lanes limited to 15 miles per hour.
GG.poles: Wooden poles along the rural lanes, often close against the hedgebank.
GG.built: Granite cottages and farmhouses with small windows and slate roofs, plus grey German concrete bunkers, gun casemates and observation towers left from the wartime occupation.
GG.nature: High earth hedgebanks along the lanes, gorse and bracken, small fields with Guernsey cattle, and cliffs with sea views along the south coast.
GG.extra: Pillar boxes are painted blue rather than red, which is a very specific Guernsey giveaway.

GH.plates: White plates with black characters where the registration ends with a dash and the two-digit year of registration. Commercial vehicles including taxis and tro-tros carry yellow plates.
GH.roads: Drives on the right. Highways have white markings and black-and-white painted kerbs, with rumble strips and heavy speed humps before every settlement and roadside police checkpoints.
GH.poles: Slender tapering concrete poles in towns and wooden poles in rural areas.
GH.built: Concrete block buildings with rust-brown corrugated iron roofs, large areas of unrendered grey blockwork, and shipping-container shops painted in telecom brand colours.
GH.nature: Strong orange-red laterite soil, oil palm, plantain and cocoa in the wet south, and drier savanna with baobab and shea in the north.
GH.extra: MTN yellow paint covers kiosks and walls, hand-painted shop signs carry religious slogans such as By His Grace, and tro-tro minibuses have slogans across the rear window.

GI.plates: UK-style plates, white at the front and yellow at the rear, with registrations beginning with the letter G.
GI.roads: Drives on the right despite being British, with UK-style road markings and signs written in English. The main road crosses the airport runway on the level, with barriers that close when aircraft land.
GI.poles: Almost no utility poles; the territory is dense and urban, with wall-mounted cabling and street lighting on the sea walls.
GI.built: Tightly packed Georgian and Victorian British terraces with sash windows and Spanish-style painted shutters, in pastel colours, crammed under a huge limestone cliff.
GI.nature: The bare grey limestone face of the Rock dominates nearly every view, with olive, pine and prickly pear on the upper slopes and Barbary macaques on the roads at the top.
GI.extra: Red pillar boxes, British pubs, Morrisons and Marks and Spencer, with the Spanish town of La Linea and its tower blocks visible immediately across the border.

GL.plates: Danish-style white plates with black characters but no EU strip.
GL.roads: Drives on the right. There are no roads at all between towns, so every road network is a short local one that simply stops at the edge of the settlement; surfaces are gravel or patched asphalt with little marking.
GL.poles: More distinctive than the poles are the insulated heat and water pipes running above ground on timber and steel trestles right alongside the roads.
