GL.built: Small timber houses painted in single strong colours of red, blue, yellow and green, raised on rock outcrops or piles, with plain concrete apartment blocks in Nuuk and Sisimiut.
GL.nature: No trees. Bare grey gneiss and granite, moss, lichen and low arctic scrub, snow patches, and icebergs or sea ice in the fjord behind the town.
GL.extra: Bilingual Greenlandic and Danish signage. North of the Arctic Circle you see sled dogs chained in lines on the edge of town.

GM.roads: Drives on the right. The main south-bank highway is smooth tarmac with white markings, while most streets are sandy orange laterite with no markings at all; signage is in English.
GM.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms are common, with concrete poles around Banjul and Serrekunda.
GM.built: Single-storey concrete block compounds with corrugated iron roofs and swept sand yards, plus whitewashed mosques with green-trimmed minarets in every village.
GM.nature: Flat land of pale orange sandy soil either side of the wide brown river, with mangrove, oil palm, mango and baobab, and groundnut fields.
GM.extra: Yellow taxis with a green stripe work local routes and plain green taxis serve tourists, and Senegal is visible or immediately adjacent in every direction.

GN.roads: Drives on the right. Signage is in French, the Conakry corridor is congested dual carriageway with faded markings, and roads upcountry are red laterite.
GN.built: Concrete block houses under corrugated iron rusted a deep orange, unfinished multi-storey frames in Conakry, and round mud huts with conical thatch in the Fouta Djallon.
GN.nature: Bauxite-red soil that stains everything, green hills and waterfalls in the Fouta Djallon, mangrove along the coast, and dense forest in the south-east.
GN.extra: Ageing Renault and Peugeot estate cars run as shared taxis, almost always overloaded with roof luggage.

GP.plates: French plates: white with black characters, a blue EU strip with F, and the department number 971 in the right-hand band.
GP.roads: Drives on the right. Complete French road furniture including N-road numbering, roundabouts and white markings, plus a short stretch of motorway around Pointe-a-Pitre.
GP.poles: Concrete poles along the main roads, with lines cut through dense vegetation.
GP.built: French supermarkets, roundabout sculptures and administrative buildings alongside Creole timber houses with fretwork and louvred shutters, and plain concrete bungalows with metal roofs.
GP.nature: Basse-Terre is mountainous rainforest with tree ferns and the Soufriere volcano, while Grande-Terre is flat, dry limestone with sugar cane and ruined stone windmills.
GP.extra: Euro prices, gendarmerie and French chain stores. Banana plantations often have bunches wrapped in blue plastic bags.

GQ.nature: Dense equatorial rainforest and oil palm over deep red laterite on the mainland, with black volcanic rock and dark sand beaches on Bioko.

GR.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and GR; three letters, a hyphen, then four digits, using only characters shared with the Latin alphabet. Front and rear are both white.
GR.roads: Warning signs have a yellow background. Motorway direction signs are green and other main roads blue, and rural highways have wide paved shoulders marked off by a solid white line that slower traffic routinely drives along.
GR.poles: Grey concrete poles with a rounded top are typical, plus plenty of wooden poles in villages; cabling is often tangled and low.
GR.built: Flat-roofed concrete apartment blocks with deep balconies and fabric awnings, very often with bare reinforcing rods left projecting from the roof for a future storey. Islands and older villages show whitewashed cubic houses with blue joinery.
GR.nature: Gnarled olive groves, dark cypress spires, Aleppo pine, oleander in central reservations, and dry pale limestone hillsides with thin red-brown soil.
GR.extra: Small roadside shrines shaped like miniature churches on a post are a strong tell. Signs put Greek above a Latin transliteration, and ΟΠΑΠ, ΚΑΦΕ and ΦΑΡΜΑΚΕΙΟ appear on shopfronts.

GS.extra: There is no permanent population beyond a handful of government staff and scientists at King Edward Point, no road network beyond a few short gravel tracks, and the only built features are the rusting Grytviken whaling station and a small white church.

GT.plates: Plates are colour and letter coded by class, with private cars carrying a P prefix on a white plate with dark characters and GUATEMALA printed across the top.
GT.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edges, on narrow winding mountain highways with steel or concrete guardrail, frequent tumulos speed bumps, and long unpaved stretches off the main routes.
GT.poles: Square and round concrete poles are the norm in towns and along highways, with wooden poles common in rural areas.
GT.built: Concrete block houses with corrugated laminate roofs, whole walls painted as adverts for mobile networks or political parties, and Spanish colonial centres with clay tile roofs and cobbled streets in Antigua.
GT.nature: Steep volcanic highlands with pine and oak forest, maize milpas planted up very steep slopes, shade-grown coffee, and hot lowland jungle in the Peten.
GT.extra: Spanish signage with many Mayan place names, brightly painted former American school buses, women in woven huipiles in the highlands, and buildings painted entirely in Tigo or Claro branding.

GU.plates: US-sized plates reading Guam USA, typically with a latte stone graphic and a red and blue design.
GU.roads: Drives on the right. Wide American-style roads with US sign shapes, green route shields, speed limits in miles per hour and heavy congestion around Tamuning and Tumon.
GU.poles: Heavy concrete utility poles built to survive typhoons, carrying American-pattern transformers.
GU.built: Low-rise reinforced concrete buildings with flat roofs and typhoon shutters, American strip malls and fast-food chains, and a cluster of high-rise hotels along Tumon Bay.
GU.nature: A limestone plateau in the north covered in dense tangantangan scrub thickets, red lateritic savanna hills in the south, coconut palms and wide reef flats.
GU.extra: Extensive US military bases and fencing, Japanese and Korean signage in the tourist district, and latte stone pillar motifs used decoratively everywhere.

GW.roads: Drives on the right. Signage is in Portuguese, and the tarmac is narrow and badly broken with almost no markings.
GW.built: Crumbling Portuguese colonial buildings with pastel render and tiled roofs in Bissau, and round mud-walled huts with thatch in the villages.
GW.nature: Flat low-lying land of mangrove creeks and tidal flats, extensive cashew orchards and oil palm, over grey-brown to reddish sandy soil.

GY.plates: White plates with black characters, typically two or three letters followed by four digits.
GY.roads: Traffic drives on the left, which with Suriname makes Guyana one of only two mainland South American countries to do so. The coastal main road is flat and narrow with white edge lines, deep drainage canals on both sides and frequent unpainted speed humps.
GY.poles: Wooden utility poles predominate along the coastal road, with concrete poles in Georgetown.
GY.built: Timber houses raised on stilts or concrete columns with corrugated zinc roofs and fretwork verandas, plus white-painted colonial wooden buildings in Georgetown.
GY.nature: A flat coastal strip of rice paddy, sugar cane and coconut behind a sea wall, with unbroken rainforest inland and no relief near the populated coast.
GY.extra: English and Guyanese Creole signage, .gy addresses, Hindu jhandi prayer flags on bamboo poles in front gardens, mandirs and mosques alongside churches, and right-hand-drive Japanese used cars.

HK.plates: White at the front and yellow at the rear with black characters and no country identifier, typically two letters then four digits.
HK.roads: Drives on the left. Double yellow lines along the kerb, yellow criss-cross box junctions, and an extraordinary density of elevated expressways, flyovers and chevron-marked ramps threaded between towers.
HK.poles: Very few utility poles in the built-up area; cabling is on building walls and in ducts, and bamboo scaffolding lashed with plastic ties covers buildings under work.
HK.built: Very tall, very slender residential towers in tight clusters, often on podium bases, with air-conditioning units, drying poles and caged windows on every facade, backed by steep green hillsides.
HK.nature: Steep forested hills immediately behind the city with concrete catchwater channels cut across them, banyan trees sending aerial roots down stone retaining walls.
HK.extra: Traditional Chinese characters, never simplified, beside English on every official sign. Taxis are red in urban areas, green in the New Territories and blue on Lantau; double-decker buses and trams are everywhere.

HM.extra: Uninhabited sub-Antarctic volcanic islands with no buildings, roads or vehicles and no street-level imagery.

HN.plates: White plates with black characters, three letters and four digits, with a blue band across the top reading HONDURAS beside the flag.
HN.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edges on main highways with narrow shoulders, frequent speed bumps, black-and-white painted kerbs, and long unpaved stretches on secondary roads.
HN.poles: Wooden poles are widespread in rural areas, with square and round concrete poles in towns and along main highways.
HN.built: Concrete block and adobe houses with corrugated zinc roofs, colonial towns with whitewashed walls and red clay tile roofs, and open-fronted pulperia shops painted in beer or soft drink branding.
HN.nature: Pine forest across the interior highlands, unusual at this latitude, with banana and oil palm on the humid north coast and dry thorn scrub in the southern Pacific lowlands.
HN.extra: Spanish signage; repainted American school buses serve as public transport and Tigo and Claro branding covers small shops.

HR.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and HR; the town code is followed by the red-and-white chequered shield, then digits and two letters, all separated by hyphens. The chequy shield in the middle of the plate is the giveaway.
HR.roads: Motorway direction signs are green and other main roads blue. Markings are white and generally in good condition, with well-maintained W-beam barriers on the coastal and mountain routes.
HR.poles: Concrete poles inland, with slimmer round concrete or metal posts along the coast; low-voltage lines are commonly strapped to house walls in old coastal towns.
HR.built: Pale limestone walls, terracotta pantiles and green wooden shutters along the Adriatic, with slim Venetian-style bell towers. Inland Slavonia has low plastered houses with hipped roofs set gable-end to the street.
HR.nature: Bright white karst limestone with maquis, cypress and Aleppo pine near the sea, red terra rossa soil in Istria, and oak and beech forest on the Pannonian side.
HR.extra: Croatian uses č, ć, š, ž and đ. Konoba, Pekara and Slastičarna appear on shopfronts, and dry stone walls divide tiny coastal fields.

HT.plates: White plates with black characters carrying HAITI and the flag, with a letter code for the vehicle class; official and aid-agency vehicles use distinct coloured plates.
HT.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Most roads carry no markings at all, surfaces are heavily broken or unpaved, and drainage ravines, rubble and informal market stalls encroach on the carriageway.
HT.poles: Concrete and wooden poles carry chaotic, heavily tangled wiring, and street lighting is largely absent or non-functional.
HT.built: Grey unrendered concrete block with flat roofs and protruding rebar, packed densely onto hillsides, interspersed with corrugated metal shacks and a few surviving French colonial gingerbread houses.
HT.nature: Severely deforested brown and eroded hillsides with sparse scrub and scattered mango trees, a sharp contrast with the wooded Dominican side of the border; cactus and dry plains in the north-west.
HT.extra: Signage in French and Haitian Creole is unique in the Americas. Brightly hand-painted tap-tap pickup buses, borlette lottery kiosks and dense roadside markets are constant.

HU.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and H and black characters; older plates read three letters, a hyphen, three digits, while newer ones use four letters, a hyphen, three digits.
HU.roads: Markings are white, motorway direction signs blue, and long straight rural roads are often planted with continuous avenues of trees. Delineator posts are white with a black top and roadside kilometre markers are frequent.
HU.poles: Slim square-section concrete poles with an angled or stepped top are very characteristic, with wooden poles on older village lines.
HU.built: The classic village house is a long narrow single-storey building set gable-end to the street, with a covered arcaded veranda running down one side into the yard. Walls are rendered white, ochre or pale blue under red pantiles; towns add socialist panel estates.
HU.nature: Extremely flat plains with maize, wheat and sunflowers, black locust (acacia) plantations, poplar windbreaks and pale loess soil.
HU.extra: Hungarian is the only language here using the double acute accents ő and ű, and the words look nothing like their neighbours. Nemzeti Dohánybolt tobacco shops with their brown signage are a reliable marker, and domains end in .hu.

ID.plates: Private plates have moved from black with white characters to white with black characters; public transport uses yellow with black and government vehicles red with white. A small sticker below the number shows the expiry month and year.
ID.roads: Drives on the left. Green signs on toll roads and blue or green elsewhere, white markings, and low concrete kerbs painted black and white on bends; rural roads are narrow with deep open drains at the edge.
ID.poles: Round or square concrete poles, plus tall slim concrete poles carrying multiple crossarms along main roads.
ID.built: Orange-red clay pantile roofs are the strongest built tell, over rendered brick houses with small front terraces and low garden walls; mosques with green or silver domes are everywhere.
ID.nature: Bright green paddy terraces, banana, coconut and teak, with dark volcanic soil and steep conical volcanoes on the horizon in Java and Sumatra.
ID.extra: Dense scooter traffic, small roadside warung stalls with plastic banners, and frequent speed bumps made of concrete or rope. Village entrance gates and flagpoles are common.

IE.plates: White plate front and rear with black characters, a blue EU strip and IRL, and the county name printed in Irish along the top edge. Format is year, county letter and a serial, such as 231-D-12345.
IE.roads: Traffic drives on the left and speed limits are in kilometres per hour. The hard shoulder on national roads is separated by a yellow broken line, motorway signs are blue, national road signs green and local signs white.
IE.poles: Thin creosoted wooden poles, often noticeably leaning, carry low-voltage lines along nearly every rural lane.
IE.built: Detached pebble-dashed bungalows painted white or cream with concrete tile or slate roofs, set in their own plot. Town streets are terraces of brightly painted rendered shopfronts with traditional hand-painted lettering.
IE.nature: Intensely green pasture cut into small fields by thick hedgerows and dry stone walls, few mature trees, yellow-flowered gorse, brown cut-over peat bog and dark blocks of Sitka spruce.
IE.extra: Direction signs show the Irish name in italics above the English in capitals. Post boxes are green, domains end in .ie, and road numbers are prefixed M, N, R or L.

IL.plates: Yellow plates front and rear with black digits and a narrow blue band on the left carrying the flag and IL. The all-numeric number is grouped in threes or twos.
IL.roads: Drives on the right. Motorway signs are green, intercity signs blue and local signs white, all trilingual in Hebrew, Arabic and English; kerbs are painted red and white for no stopping and blue and white for permit parking.
IL.poles: Concrete and galvanised steel poles, with much of the urban distribution network on slim steel columns.
IL.built: Pale limestone cladding is mandatory in Jerusalem and common elsewhere, over flat-roofed concrete blocks; roofs carry black solar water-heater panels and white cylindrical tanks almost universally.
IL.nature: Mediterranean scrub and planted Aleppo pine on terraced rocky hillsides, cypress and eucalyptus along roads, and pale stony desert in the Negev.
IL.extra: Solar water heaters on every roof and the red-and-white kerb paint are the fastest confirmations. Bus stops, bollards and street furniture are notably standardised nationwide.

IM.plates: UK-style white front and yellow rear plates with registrations ending in the letters MAN.
IM.roads: Drives on the left. Many rural roads have no speed limit, so you see the national derestriction sign with no number on it, and stretches of the TT course carry painted kerbs, marshal posts and safety bales.
IM.poles: Wooden poles along rural roads and across open moorland.
IM.built: Grey stone and rendered Victorian terraces along the Douglas promenade, whitewashed cottages with slate roofs inland, and grey stone churches.
IM.nature: Treeless heather and gorse moorland over the central hills, small hedged and stone-walled fields lower down, and wooded glens with sycamore and ash.
IM.extra: The Manx triskelion of three armoured legs appears on signs and official markings, place-name signs are bilingual with Manx Gaelic, and electric tram and steam railway tracks cross the roads.

IN.plates: White plates with black characters for private vehicles, yellow with black for taxis and commercial vehicles, and green with white for electric vehicles. The format is a two-letter state code, district number, a letter series and four digits.
IN.roads: Drives on the left. National highway signs are green with white text and other direction signs are blue or white; kerbs and roadside trees are painted in black-and-white or yellow-and-black bands, and median barriers are low concrete.
IN.poles: Square or round concrete poles and slim steel lattice masts, with dense untidy cable bundles and street lights on curved brackets.
IN.built: Flat-roofed concrete buildings with exposed reinforcement bars waiting for another storey, painted in strong colours, with rolling steel shutters on ground-floor shops.
IN.nature: Ranges from dry thorn scrub and red-brown soil in the centre to irrigated wheat plains in the north and coconut and banana in the south; neem, banyan and eucalyptus line many roads.
IN.extra: Brightly painted Tata and Ashok Leyland trucks with Horn OK Please lettering, three-wheeled auto-rickshaws in green-and-yellow or black-and-yellow, and roadside shrines with marigold garlands.

IO.roads: Drives on the left. The only roads are inside the joint UK and US military base on Diego Garcia and are closed to the public.
IO.extra: There is no civilian population and access is restricted to military and contractor personnel, so no public street-level imagery exists.

IQ.plates: White plates with black characters and the governorate name in Arabic; the Kurdistan Region issues its own separate design. Layouts have changed several times so older styles are still in circulation.
IQ.roads: Drives on the right. Wide highways with green direction signs in Arabic above English, worn white markings, and concrete Jersey barriers used heavily as both median and security barrier.
IQ.poles: Concrete and steel poles carrying heavy cable bundles, with a very large number of informal generator cables strung between buildings.
IQ.built: Beige and sand-coloured concrete and breeze block with flat roofs, roof water tanks, and shopfronts under wide metal canopies; brickwork is common in the north.
IQ.nature: Flat dusty alluvial plain with date palm groves along the rivers and irrigation canals, drier gravel desert to the west and green rolling hills in the Kurdish north.
IQ.extra: Grey concrete T-wall blast barriers, checkpoints with sandbags, and party or religious flags and portraits on lamp posts are pervasive. Older Toyotas and pickups dominate.

IR.plates: White plates with black Persian numerals and a single Persian letter, with a narrow blue band on the left carrying the flag and I.R.IRAN; taxis and public vehicles use yellow plates.
IR.roads: Drives on the right. Freeway signs are green with white text in Persian above English, with generous white markings, concrete Jersey barriers in the central reservation and frequent overhead gantries.
IR.poles: Concrete poles in towns and galvanised steel lattice masts along highways, with substantial street lighting even on rural roads.
IR.built: Beige and buff brick or rendered concrete with flat roofs, roof-top water tanks and air coolers, and turquoise-tiled domes and minarets in older quarters.
IR.nature: Dry brown and grey mountains with little cover over most of the country, poplars and plane trees lining irrigated roads, and dense green forest on the Caspian slope in the north.
IR.extra: Locally built Saipa Pride hatchbacks, Peugeot 405 and Samand saloons make up most traffic. Large painted murals and portraits appear on the blank end walls of buildings.

IS.plates: White plate with a blue strip on the left carrying the national flag and IS, black characters, two letters then three digits.
IS.roads: Warning signs have a yellow background, and the road edge is marked by tall posts with yellow reflective tops. Many rural bridges are single lane with a warning sign, and away from the ring road surfaces turn to graded gravel.
IS.poles: Wooden poles and small steel lattice structures carry lines across open ground; long stretches of country have no overhead wiring at all.
IS.built: Houses clad in corrugated steel sheeting, painted in strong reds, blues and greens with matching corrugated roofs, plus plain rendered concrete boxes. Settlements are small, low and treeless.
IS.nature: Black basalt gravel and lava fields carpeted in pale green moss, almost no trees, purple lupin swathes in summer, glacier tongues, waterfalls and rust-brown tussock grass.
IS.extra: Icelandic uses the letters þ and ð, which no other European language does. Sheep roam loose beside the road and route numbers appear in plain boxes on yellow-topped posts.

IT.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and I on the left and a second blue band on the right carrying the two-letter province code above the year of registration. Format is two letters, three digits, two letters.
IT.roads: Motorway direction signs are green and all other main roads are signed in blue. Markings are white with yellow used for bus lanes, and guardrails are a rounded-profile W-beam on tight concrete or steel posts.
IT.poles: Round tapered concrete poles with a smooth finish are the usual rural carrier; in old towns the cable is clipped to building walls on iron brackets.
IT.built: Ochre, terracotta and pastel-rendered walls under roman pantile roofs, with louvred shutters and external roller blinds. Narrow stone-paved streets, arcades, and a campanile on the skyline of almost every town.
IT.nature: Cypress spires, olive groves, vineyards on trellises, umbrella pines near the coast, Alpine spruce in the far north, and dry scrubby maquis in the south.
IT.extra: A blue sign with a large white T marks tabacchi shops and is an instant giveaway. Town entry signs are white with the comune name, and domains end in .it.

JE.plates: UK-style white front and yellow rear plates with registrations starting with the letter J followed by digits.
JE.roads: Drives on the left with a 40 miles per hour island maximum and 15 miles per hour Green Lanes. Junctions use yellow filter-in-turn arrows and solid yellow lines painted across the mouth of side roads instead of give-way triangles.
JE.poles: Wooden poles along the rural lanes, tight against high earth banks.
JE.built: Pink and grey granite farmhouses with rounded arch doorways and steep roofs, plus German occupation bunkers on the headlands and round Jersey coastal towers.
JE.nature: Steep south-facing cotil slopes planted with Jersey Royal potatoes, high hedgebanks, small fields and Jersey cattle.
JE.extra: Road names are in French, with Rue, Mont and La Route used throughout, while everything else is in English. Pillar boxes are red, unlike Guernsey's blue ones.

JM.plates: White plates with black characters, typically four digits and two letters. Public passenger vehicles and taxis carry red plates with white characters, which is a quick confirmation.
JM.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Roads are narrow with broken edges, deep open concrete gutters beside the carriageway and frequent large speed bumps; main A-roads carry white edge lines and white centre lines where marked at all.
JM.poles: Wooden utility poles carrying many lines, often noticeably leaning, close to the road edge.
JM.built: Concrete block houses with flat or zinc roofs, unpainted block and rebar on unfinished builds, and zinc-sheet fenced yards; roadside bars and shops painted in Digicel red or Red Stripe branding.
JM.nature: Lush and green, with limestone karst hills, bamboo arching over rural roads, banana, breadfruit and mango, and dry cactus scrub along the south coast.
JM.extra: English and Jamaican Patois signage, .jm and .com.jm addresses, hand-painted shop signs, and jerk pans made from cut oil drums at the roadside.

JO.plates: White plates with black numerals split into a small code group and a larger number; taxis and public service vehicles use green plates.
JO.roads: Drives on the right. Blue and green direction signs with Arabic above English, brown signs for archaeological sites, and very frequent unmarked speed bumps in towns.
JO.poles: Concrete and steel poles carrying overhead cable in towns and villages.
JO.built: Hillsides covered in near-identical beige limestone and rendered blocks with flat roofs, black plastic water tanks and white solar heaters on top, and unfinished top floors with protruding rebar.
JO.nature: Dry rocky plateau with pale tan and pink stone, olive and pine plantations in the wetter north, and bare gravel and sand desert east and south.
JO.extra: Black roof water tanks are near-universal. Traffic is dominated by older Japanese and Korean saloons, with many Hyundai and Kia taxis.

JP.plates: White plates with green characters for ordinary private cars, yellow plates with black for kei cars, and green plates with white for commercial vehicles. The issuing city name appears in small kanji at the top left.
JP.roads: Drives on the left. Expressway signs are green and ordinary road signs blue, both with kanji above romaji; centre lines are yellow where overtaking is banned and white elsewhere, and the stop sign is an inverted red triangle reading tomare.
JP.poles: Round tapering concrete poles are everywhere, closely spaced, carrying transformers, and often set right at the edge of the carriageway with no pavement.
JP.built: Narrow two-storey houses packed tightly together, grey or blue ceramic tiled roofs, corrugated metal cladding, and blue plastic tarpaulins over older roofs.
JP.nature: Steep hills covered in dark planted sugi cedar and cypress, bamboo groves, rice paddies on every flat surface, and deciduous forest in the mountains.
JP.extra: Yellow raised tactile paving, vending machines standing alone at roadsides, red-and-white striped snow poles and overhead arrows in the north, and mirrors on blind corners.

KE.plates: White front, yellow rear, black characters, format three letters then three digits then a letter. Government vehicles use red plates.
KE.roads: Drives on the left. Yellow edge lines with a white broken centre line are the classic combination. Speed bumps are extremely frequent through settlements.
KE.poles: Slim concrete poles, often with a visible seam, plus many wooden poles in rural areas.
KE.built: Corrugated iron roofs over concrete block walls, brightly painted shopfronts advertising mobile money agents.
KE.nature: Red lateritic soil, acacia savanna, tea and coffee on the highlands, roadside sisal.
KE.extra: Matatu minibuses covered in airbrushed art, and Safaricom green paint on kiosks along almost every road.

KG.plates: White plates with black characters and a blue band on the left showing KG and the flag, with a two-digit region code at the start.
KG.roads: Drives on the right. Blue direction signs with white text, patchy white markings, and mountain passes with hairpins, concrete kerb blocks and only intermittent guardrail.
KG.poles: Grey concrete poles, frequently leaning, with older wooden poles on village lanes and lattice steel towers near hydro schemes.
KG.built: Single-storey houses with rendered or mud-brick walls and shallow painted metal roofs, with sky-blue painted window frames, gates and fences recurring throughout.
KG.nature: High snow-capped Tien Shan ranges above green alpine pasture, spruce on north-facing slopes, walnut forest in the south-west, and poplar rows in the valleys.
KG.extra: Yurts and livestock appear on summer pastures and beside passes. A large share of cars are right-hand-drive Japanese imports despite right-hand traffic, and Soviet mosaic bus shelters survive on rural roads.

KH.plates: White plates with black characters, the province name in Khmer along the top and a blue vertical band on the left carrying KH and the flag.
KH.roads: Drives on the right. Main highways have white edge lines and a broken white centre line, with blue and white direction signs in Khmer above Latin; many secondary roads are bare red laterite.
KH.poles: Square concrete poles with a tapering profile, very similar to Thailand, often leaning and heavily loaded with cable.
KH.built: Narrow concrete shophouses with shuttered balconies, corrugated metal roofs, and timber houses raised on stilts with the space beneath used for storage.
KH.nature: Flat paddy plains studded with tall sugar palms with their distinctive fan crowns, plus dry dipterocarp forest and bright red-orange laterite soil.
KH.extra: An unusually high proportion of Lexus RX SUVs and Toyota Camrys, plus motorbike trailers used as taxis. Red dust coats roadside vegetation in the dry season.

KI.roads: Drives on the left. One narrow sealed road runs the length of South Tarawa, crossing causeways between islets, with almost no lane markings and lagoon or open ocean visible on both sides at once.
KI.poles: Short concrete and timber poles set close to the road carrying a single low line of cable.
KI.built: Low buildings of concrete block or timber with rusting corrugated-iron roofs, interspersed with open-sided thatched maneaba meeting houses on coral platforms.
KI.nature: Coconut palms and pandanus on a strip of white coral sand and rubble, with no hills at all and an entirely flat horizon.
KI.extra: The land is so narrow that water is usually visible on both sides of the road, and buildings crowd right up to the carriageway in South Tarawa.

KM.roads: Drives on the right. Narrow potholed tarmac with almost no markings, winding between villages and along the shoreline.
KM.built: Breeze-block and coral-stone houses with corrugated iron roofs, a whitewashed mosque with a green-trimmed minaret in nearly every village, and carved Swahili doors in Moroni's stone town.
KM.nature: Dark volcanic rock and black sand beaches, dense green coconut, banana, mango and clove, and the bare cone of Karthala rising above Grande Comore.

KN.plates: White plates with black characters and a leading letter marking the vehicle class.
KN.roads: Traffic drives on the left. The island ring roads are narrow and lightly marked, kerbless in places, with concrete drains alongside and speed bumps through villages.
KN.poles: Wooden utility poles carrying a few lines are the standard.
KN.built: Small concrete and timber houses with corrugated metal roofs and painted shutters, plus tall stone chimneys and dry stone walls surviving from abandoned sugar estates.
KN.nature: A steep central volcanic cone under rainforest above a skirt of former cane fields now gone to grass and scrub, with coconut palms and tamarind along the coast; vervet monkeys are often at the roadside.
KN.extra: English signage, East Caribbean dollar prices and right-hand-drive Japanese used cars.

KP.roads: Drives on the right. Main highways are wide concrete slab carriageways with joints and grass growing between them, almost no markings, no lighting and virtually no traffic.
KP.built: Pastel-painted concrete apartment blocks in regimented rows, single-storey tiled-roof houses in villages, and large propaganda murals and slogan boards at road junctions.
KP.nature: Heavily deforested brown hills terraced right to the summits, maize and rice fields worked by hand, with pine plantations on some slopes.
KP.extra: Imagery is extremely limited and mostly taken from tour buses or trains. Pedestrians and cyclists vastly outnumber cars, and traffic officers stand at junctions.

KR.plates: White plates with black Hangul and digits for private cars, yellow with black for commercial vehicles and buses, and blue with white for electric vehicles. Newer plates carry a small holographic emblem on the left.
KR.roads: Drives on the right. Expressway signs are green and national road signs blue, with Hangul above English; centre lines are yellow, bus lanes are marked in blue, and crossings and junctions use extensive coloured surfacing.
KR.poles: Round tapering concrete poles very similar to Japan's, densely spaced, plus slim steel columns with curved lighting arms in newer districts.
KR.built: Huge clusters of identical high-rise apartment towers, each with a large block number painted near the top, rise even beside small towns; low-rise areas are brick or tiled four-storey villa buildings with rooftop structures.
KR.nature: Steep granite hills covered in pine and mixed deciduous forest right up to the edge of towns, with small rice paddies filling every flat valley floor.
KR.extra: Hyundai and Kia make up most traffic. Green mesh fencing, stainless steel pedestrian railings painted in bright colours, and extensive roadside advertising in Hangul are constant.

KW.plates: White plates with black digits and a small category letter, with the country name in Arabic and English; front and rear match.
KW.roads: Drives on the right. Very wide multi-lane highways with green direction signs in Arabic above English, heavy use of concrete barriers, and large numbered roundabouts and interchanges.
KW.built: Large boxy villas in beige or white render with flat roofs, decorative concrete screens and high boundary walls, arranged in strict rectangular blocks.
KW.nature: Utterly flat pale sand and gravel desert with no natural trees; roadside greenery is irrigated planted palms, oleander and clipped shrubs.
KW.extra: Sand blows across the carriageway and stains the kerbs. Traffic is overwhelmingly large white and silver Japanese and American SUVs.

KY.plates: Reflective plates carrying the words Cayman Islands and a green sea turtle graphic, which is a strong and specific tell.
KY.roads: Drives on the left. Grand Cayman is very flat with wide, smooth, well-maintained sealed roads, numerous roundabouts, British-style signage and a stretch of dual carriageway on the Esterley Tibbetts Highway.
KY.poles: Concrete poles on newer roads and wooden poles on older ones, with some services placed underground in resort areas.
KY.built: Modern low-rise concrete condominiums, banks and offices along Seven Mile Beach, with pastel Caymanian cottages with shingle or metal roofs and white picket fences in the older districts.
KY.nature: Flat and dry with sea grape, casuarina, silver thatch palms and mangrove, and jagged black ironshore limestone at the shoreline.
KY.extra: British roundabouts and road markings combined with American vehicles, US dollar pricing and a conspicuous density of bank and law firm signage.

KZ.plates: White plates with black characters, three digits, three letters and a two-digit region code, with a narrow blue band on the right carrying KZ and the flag.
KZ.roads: Drives on the right. Long straight roads with white markings, blue direction signs with white text and green on the main corridors, and almost no guardrail across open steppe.
KZ.poles: Grey concrete poles, often with a distinctive slim tapered profile, spaced widely along the roadside with long slack spans.
KZ.built: Soviet-era five-storey panel blocks in towns, plus single-storey houses with rendered walls painted white or pale blue and shallow pitched painted metal roofs.
KZ.nature: Vast flat grass and feather-grass steppe with almost no trees, semi-desert and salt flats in the south, and birch stands in the far north.
KZ.extra: Planted windbreak rows of poplar or elm run parallel to roads and railways. Lada saloons and Soviet-era buses remain common outside the big cities.

LA.plates: Private vehicles use yellow plates with black characters; state vehicles use blue with white and military red with white. The province name appears in Lao script.
LA.roads: Drives on the right. Mostly narrow two-lane roads with faded or absent markings, blue and white direction signs in Lao above Latin, and long unsealed red-earth sections.
LA.poles: Square tapered concrete poles carrying a small number of lines, with timber poles still in use in remoter districts.
LA.built: Timber houses raised on stilts with corrugated roofs, plain concrete shophouses in towns, and French colonial shuttered buildings with stucco in Vientiane and Luang Prabang.
LA.nature: Dramatic grey limestone karst towers in the north, teak and bamboo forest, terraced and lowland paddy, and deep red laterite soil and dust.
LA.extra: Temple compounds with steep multi-tiered roofs and naga balustrades, Beerlao signage on shopfronts, and very light traffic with many small trucks and two-wheeled walking tractors.

LB.plates: White plates with red characters and a small cedar emblem, with the country name in Arabic and Latin; public service vehicles use red plates with white characters.
LB.roads: Drives on the right. Green and blue direction signs with Arabic above Latin, often bilingual Arabic-French, with heavily worn markings, steep switchbacks and inconsistent guardrail.
LB.poles: Concrete and steel poles carrying extremely dense tangles of cable, with additional private generator wiring strung between buildings and across streets.
LB.built: Dense unrendered concrete apartment blocks stacked up steep slopes, older sandstone houses with triple-arched windows and red clay pantile roofs, and many buildings still pitted with shell and bullet damage.
LB.nature: Mediterranean pine, oak and olive on steep terraced slopes, citrus and banana on the coastal strip, and bare rocky ridges with snow in winter.
LB.extra: Private diesel generators and their cable runs are ubiquitous. Political party flags, portraits and posters cover lamp posts and walls, differing sharply between neighbourhoods.

LC.plates: White plates with black characters and a leading letter marking the vehicle class.
LC.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Roads are extremely steep and serpentine with tight hairpins, little or no centre marking, deep roadside concrete gutters and frequent landslip repairs.
LC.poles: Wooden utility poles set into steep banks at the road edge are the norm.
LC.built: Concrete houses with metal roofs stepped into hillsides and painted in strong colours, with older timber houses and French-influenced fretwork in Soufriere and Castries.
LC.nature: Densely forested volcanic peaks including the twin Pitons, banana plantations filling the valleys, coconut and mango, and steep ravines running straight to the sea.
LC.extra: English signage alongside Kweyol speech and strongly French place names such as Soufriere, Micoud and Gros Islet; right-hand-drive Japanese imports and East Caribbean dollar prices.

LI.plates: Black plate with white characters, the princely coat of arms on the left and the letters FL. The black background makes it unmistakable.
LI.roads: Road signage follows the Swiss pattern, with green signs for motorway destinations and blue for other main roads. Pedestrian crossings are painted yellow rather than white, and markings are otherwise white with yellow used for restrictions.
LI.built: A mixture of modern white-rendered houses with wide-eaved roofs and timber balconies on the valley slopes, tidy light-industrial units on the flat, and a hilltop castle above the main town.
LI.nature: A flat Rhine valley floor of maize and pasture, rising abruptly into steep forested slopes of spruce and beech with rock faces above.
LI.extra: German signage in Swiss orthography, with no ß in use. Prices are in Swiss francs and there are no border controls with Switzerland.

LK.plates: Front plates are white with black characters and rear plates yellow with black; the province is shown by a two-letter code, and commercial vehicles use different colour combinations.
LK.roads: Drives on the left. Narrow winding roads with white edge lines, low whitewashed kerb stones and painted concrete bollards, and trilingual signs in Sinhala, Tamil and English.
LK.poles: Square tapered concrete poles and older timber poles, carrying relatively light cable along the roadside.
LK.built: Single-storey houses with terracotta or corrugated roofs and small verandas, colonial-era shuttered buildings in towns, and whitewashed dome-shaped Buddhist dagobas.
LK.nature: Coconut palms and paddy in the lowlands, clipped tea bushes on terraced slopes in the central hills, dense rainforest in the south-west, and strong red laterite soil.
LK.extra: Bajaj tuk-tuks in every colour are everywhere. Buddhist prayer flags, small roadside shrines with images of the Buddha under bo trees, and long-distance buses with loud liveries are typical.

LR.plates: White plates with black characters and the word Liberia across the top.
LR.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are in English, Monrovia's main roads have faded white markings, and most of the country runs on deep red laterite that turns to thick mud in the rains.
LR.poles: Wooden poles and slim concrete poles around Monrovia, with many roads carrying no line at all.
LR.built: Zinc-roofed timber and concrete block houses, war-damaged concrete shells still standing in Monrovia, and American-influenced verandas with wooden shutters in the older settler towns.
LR.nature: Dense green rainforest and enormous rubber plantations over deep red-orange laterite, with standing water and mud along the verges for much of the year.
LR.extra: Yellow taxis and yellow keke tricycles in Monrovia, American English spellings on signs, and prices quoted in both US and Liberian dollars.

LS.plates: White reflective plates with black characters.
LS.roads: Drives on the left. Tarmac roads carry white centre lines and yellow edge lines with armco barriers on the passes, and a dense network of graded gravel tracks climbs into the mountains.
LS.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms along the valley roads, with concrete poles around Maseru.
LS.built: Stone and concrete block houses with corrugated iron roofs painted green or red, round thatched rondavels, and dry-stone kraals; almost every building sits on a slope.
LS.nature: Treeless high-altitude grassland in gold and brown, deeply eroded red-brown donga gullies, basalt cliffs and peaks, and willows and poplars along the streams.
LS.extra: Men on horseback wrapped in Basotho blankets and wearing conical grass hats, and South African branding in the shops.

LT.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and LT and black characters, formatted as three letters, a space and three digits.
LT.roads: Markings are white, warning triangles have a white background, and main roads are frequently lined with dense avenues of trees. Rural crossroads often carry a carved wooden cross or shrine on a post.
LT.poles: Grey concrete poles are the norm, often round and tapered, and large white stork nests built on top of poles and platforms are extremely common.
LT.built: Painted timber village houses with decorated eaves, Soviet-era apartment blocks, twin-towered baroque Catholic churches, and red-brick Gothic in Vilnius and Kaunas.
LT.nature: Flat or gently undulating farmland broken by mixed pine and birch woodland, small lakes, and sandy soils near the coast.
LT.extra: Lithuanian uses ė, ų and ž and nearly every noun ends in -as, -is or -us. Roadside wooden crucifixes and folk carvings are a cultural constant, and domains end in .lt.

LU.plates: Yellow plate front and rear with black characters and a blue EU strip with L. The yellow-at-both-ends combination narrows it down fast.
LU.roads: Markings are white and motorway direction signs blue; the road network is dense, well surfaced and heavily signed for such a small area. Route numbers are prefixed A, N or CR.
LU.poles: Distribution is largely underground; overhead lines are uncommon along main roads.
LU.built: Grey slate roofs over stone or rendered walls in the Ardennes north, and dense stone-built quarters around deep rocky gorges in the capital. Newer housing is neat, uniform and rendered in pale colours.
LU.nature: Rolling wooded hills of beech and spruce in the north, open farmland in the centre, and steep terraced vineyards along the Moselle in the east.
LU.extra: Street signs are in French (Rue, Avenue) and other signage is often French and German together, with Luxembourgish appearing on place-name signs. Fuel is conspicuously cheap and border filling stations are huge; domains end in .lu.

LV.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and LV and black characters, most commonly two letters, a hyphen and four digits. Front and rear are the same.
LV.roads: Markings are white and warning triangles have a white background. Many minor roads are unsealed gravel, and paved rural roads typically have a narrow shoulder dropping straight into a mown verge and ditch.
LV.poles: Weathered grey wooden poles predominate in the countryside, with concrete posts on newer or higher-capacity lines.
LV.built: Timber farmhouses and outbuildings with board cladding, Soviet-era brick and panel blocks on town edges, red brick Lutheran churches, and elaborate Art Nouveau facades in Riga.
LV.nature: Flat land with pine and birch forest, wet meadows and bogs, sandy pale soil, and isolated farmsteads standing alone in open fields rather than clustered in villages.
LV.extra: Latvian marks long vowels with macrons (ā, ē, ī, ū) and uses comma-accented ģ, ķ, ļ and ņ, and nearly every place name ends in -s. Domains end in .lv.

LY.plates: White plates with black characters in both Arabic and Latin, newer issues carrying a coloured band on the left.
LY.roads: Drives on the right. The coastal highway is wide with faded white markings, signs are in Arabic with some English, and kerbs are often painted black and white.
LY.poles: Concrete poles along the coastal roads with steel lattice pylons crossing the desert.
LY.built: Flat-roofed concrete and breeze-block buildings in sand and cream render, Italian colonial arcades in Tripoli and Benghazi, and a great deal of stalled construction.
LY.nature: Sand and stony grey desert over almost the whole country, with a thin green coastal strip of olive, date palm and eucalyptus.

MA.plates: White plates with black characters made up of digits, an Arabic letter and a regional number separated by dashes, the same front and rear.
MA.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are bilingual Arabic and French with Tifinagh added on many newer ones, motorway panels are green, and kerbstones are painted black-and-white or red-and-white.
MA.poles: Concrete poles with a visible casting seam in towns, and steel lattice pylons across open country.
MA.built: Ochre, pink and sand-coloured render with green-tiled pitched roofs on official buildings, flat-roofed concrete housing, and mud-brick kasbahs and ksour in the south.
MA.nature: Reddish-brown soil with olive, argan and prickly pear, cedar and pine on the Atlas slopes, and date palm oases set against bare rock beyond the mountains.
MA.extra: Small petit taxi saloons colour-coded by city, ageing Mercedes 240D grand taxis, and donkeys with panniers on rural roads.

MC.plates: White plate with black characters and the red-and-white lozenge shield of the principality on the left, without an EU strip.
MC.roads: A compact, steeply stacked network of ramps, tunnels and multi-level streets with immaculate surfaces, white markings and French-style signage. Kerbs, planting and street furniture are conspicuously well kept.
MC.built: High-rise apartment towers in white and glass terraced down a steep slope to a yacht harbour, with Belle Époque stone facades around the casino quarter and clipped, heavily planted public spaces.
MC.nature: Steep pale limestone cliffs rising immediately behind the built-up strip, with palms, bougainvillea, oleander and other planted Mediterranean species rather than wild vegetation.
MC.extra: Signage is in French and many vehicles carry French registrations. Expect an unusually high concentration of supercars, security cameras and uniformed police.

MD.plates: White plate with a blue strip on the left carrying the national flag and MD, black characters, typically three letters and three digits.
MD.roads: Surfaces range from resurfaced main corridors to badly broken and patched secondary roads; markings are white and frequently worn away entirely. Direction signs are blue and tree trunks along the road are often whitewashed to head height.
MD.poles: Grey concrete poles, both round tapered and square-section types, are everywhere, with sagging cables and improvised connections.
MD.built: Single-storey rural houses rendered in white, pale blue or green with decorative pressed-metal porches and gates, under corrugated or metal-tile roofs. Chișinău and larger towns are dominated by Soviet-era blocks.
MD.nature: Rolling hills covered in vineyards and orchards, walnut trees lining the roads, large maize and sunflower fields and very dark chernozem soil.
MD.extra: Signage is Romanian in Latin script, switching to Cyrillic in the Transnistrian strip along the Dniester. Decorated roadside wells and carved wooden crosses at crossroads are typical; domains end in .md.

ME.plates: White plate with a blue strip and MNE on the left; the two-letter town code is followed by a small coat of arms, then two letters and three digits.
ME.roads: Narrow, tightly winding mountain and coastal roads with many unlit tunnels, frequent rockfall netting and white markings that are often faded. Motorway direction signs are green, other main roads blue.
ME.poles: Grey concrete poles carry most rural lines, with wooden poles on older village spurs.
ME.built: Stone houses with grey stone-slab or terracotta roofs and green shutters around the Bay of Kotor and the old coastal towns, and unfinished concrete-frame apartment blocks along the newer coastal strip and inland.
ME.nature: Dramatic grey karst limestone with almost no soil, deep blue inlets, black pine and beech forest on the high plateaus, and Mediterranean maquis at sea level.
ME.extra: Signs appear in both Latin and Cyrillic in places. Konoba and Pekara shopfronts are common and domains end in .me.

MF.plates: French-style white plates with black characters, mixing freely with Sint Maarten plates because the internal border is completely open.
MF.roads: Drives on the right on both halves of the island, with no border checks at all and only a small welcome monument marking the boundary; the French side uses French markings and signage.
MF.poles: Wooden poles with heavy sagging cable bundles along the coast roads.
MF.built: Marigot has French-Caribbean shophouses with shutters and awnings and an open market, with concrete villas terraced up the hillsides and some buildings still showing hurricane damage.
MF.nature: Dry, steep scrubby hills with cactus and acacia, salt ponds behind the beaches, and white sand bays.
MF.extra: Euro prices and French signage change abruptly to US dollars and Dutch text as you cross into Sint Maarten, which is the key recognition trick.

MG.plates: White plates with black characters, four digits then three letters. Older vehicles still carry black plates with white characters.
MG.roads: Drives on the right. The RN routes are narrow tarmac with no edge lines and frequent potholes, signage is in French and Malagasy, and speed humps guard every village.
MG.poles: Slim concrete poles and many leaning wooden poles, with low-hanging lines through the villages.
MG.built: Two-storey red fired-brick houses with steep tiled roofs and small wooden balconies in the highlands, a very un-African look, with palm-thatch and stilted timber huts in the coastal lowlands.
MG.nature: Brick-red lateritic soil and badly eroded bare hillsides, terraced rice paddies in the highlands, travellers palms and baobabs, and spiny octopus trees in the arid south.
MG.extra: Zebu cattle carts on the tarmac, white Mercedes and Mazda taxi-brousse minibuses, and roadside sacks of charcoal for sale.

MH.roads: Drives on the right. A single main road runs the length of Majuro atoll, sealed and kerbed in places with faded markings, with the lagoon on one side and the ocean surf on the other.
MH.poles: Concrete poles along the main road, often with American-style pole-mounted transformers.
MH.built: Single-storey buildings of concrete block and plywood with corrugated-iron roofs, water tanks beside them, and a few larger US-funded school and government buildings.
MH.nature: Coconut palms, breadfruit and a little pandanus on flat coral sand, with coral rubble shorelines and no relief whatsoever.
MH.extra: Strong American influence is visible in pickup trucks, US-style road signs and dollar pricing despite the Pacific setting.

MK.plates: White plate with a blue strip and NMK on the left; the town code is followed by digits and two letters. Older plates show MK instead.
MK.roads: Motorway direction signs are green and other main roads blue. Markings are white and often worn, secondary roads are heavily patched, and roadside kerbs and tree trunks are frequently whitewashed.
MK.poles: Grey concrete poles, many square in section with holes down the shaft, carry most distribution.
MK.built: Unfinished houses of red brick within exposed concrete frames under red pantiles are very common. Old bazaar quarters keep Ottoman houses with a jettied timber upper floor, and Skopje mixes brutalist concrete with recent neoclassical facades and statues.
MK.nature: Dry rocky hills with sparse scrub, eroded pale brown gullies, poplar rows along watercourses, tobacco and pepper fields, and deep blue lakes in the south-west.
MK.extra: Macedonian Cyrillic uses ѓ, ќ, џ and ѕ; western areas add Albanian in Latin script on the same signs. Domains end in .mk.

ML.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are in French, the main routes are single-carriageway tarmac with a white centre line and black-and-white painted kerbs, and everything else is sand or laterite piste.
ML.poles: Concrete poles in Bamako and wooden poles along the rural roads.
ML.built: Mud-brick banco architecture with flat roofs and protruding wooden toron beams along the Niger valley, with concrete block and corrugated iron in the cities.
ML.nature: Pale to orange sandy soil, Sahelian thorn scrub with acacia, baobab and shea, and true desert north of the Niger bend.
ML.extra: Green Sotrama minibuses and enormous numbers of small motorcycles fill Bamako's streets.

MM.plates: White plates with black characters on newer vehicles and older black plates with white characters still in use, with Burmese numerals and a regional prefix.
MM.roads: Drives on the right, but most cars are right-hand drive Japanese imports, so drivers sit on the kerb side and bus doors open into the middle of the road. Markings are faded white, and direction signs are blue or white in Burmese above English.
MM.poles: Concrete poles of square section in towns, with timber poles and bamboo props common in rural areas.
MM.built: Corrugated metal roofs over timber and bamboo houses, plain concrete shophouses with shuttered upper floors, and gilded stupas with white bases visible above the treeline in almost every town.
MM.nature: Paddy and toddy palms across the central dry zone with pale dusty soil, teak and monsoon forest in the hills, and dense green delta vegetation in the south.
MM.extra: People wearing longyi and the pale yellow thanaka paste on faces, betel-stained red marks on pavements, and roadside monasteries with monks in maroon robes.

MN.plates: White plates with black characters and a small blue band on the left carrying MN and the flag, with Cyrillic letters in the series.
MN.roads: Drives on the right. Few paved roads, and those that exist are narrow with white markings and no hard shoulder; elsewhere braided dirt tracks fan out across open ground with no signage at all.
MN.poles: Concrete poles along paved corridors and simple timber poles serving ger districts, often with long slack spans across empty ground.
MN.built: Ulaanbaatar has Soviet blocks and glass towers, but the characteristic texture is the ger district: white felt gers and small timber houses each inside a square plank fence painted blue, green or left bare.
MN.nature: Treeless rolling grass steppe running to the horizon, gravel and scrub in the Gobi to the south, and larch forest on north-facing slopes near the Siberian border.
MN.extra: Ovoo cairns draped in blue silk scarves sit on passes and hilltops, and herds of sheep, goats and horses regularly cross the road. Toyota Priuses and Land Cruisers dominate, many right-hand drive.

MO.plates: Black plates with white characters, usually two letters then two pairs of digits, which is immediately distinctive.
MO.roads: Drives on the left. Very narrow one-way streets in the old core, wave-patterned black and white mosaic calcada paving on the footpaths, and huge multi-level flyovers serving the Cotai casinos.
MO.poles: Almost no utility poles; instead ornate Portuguese-pattern lamp standards and dense wall-mounted cabling in the old streets.
MO.built: Pastel Portuguese colonial buildings with white plaster mouldings and azulejo tiles sit directly against very dense grey residential towers and enormous themed casino resorts.
MO.nature: Little vegetation beyond banyan trees shading old squares and the small green hills of Guia and Coloane.
MO.extra: Street name plaques are blue and white tiles giving the name in Chinese and Portuguese, even though almost nobody speaks Portuguese.

MP.plates: US-sized plates reading Northern Mariana Islands, usually with the Hafa Adai greeting.
MP.roads: Drives on the right. US-style signage and speed limits in miles per hour on Saipan's Beach Road and Middle Road, with rough potholed surfaces on the minor roads.
MP.poles: Heavy concrete typhoon-rated poles with American-pattern transformers.
MP.built: Low concrete buildings with flat roofs and typhoon shutters, Japanese, Korean and Chinese shop signage in Garapan, and ruined Japanese wartime concrete structures left in place.
MP.nature: Dense tangantangan scrub thickets covering the limestone hills, coconut palms along the coast, and high cliffs at the northern ends of Saipan and Tinian.
MP.extra: Very heavy East Asian tourist signage combined with American road design, plus numerous Second World War memorials and rusting relics.

MQ.plates: French plates: white with black characters, a blue EU strip with F, and the department number 972 in the right-hand band.
MQ.roads: Drives on the right. Standard French markings and signage, with a dual carriageway between Fort-de-France and Le Lamentin and tight hairpin climbs through the northern hills.
MQ.poles: Concrete poles along the main roads.
MQ.built: Creole houses with fretwork verandahs and corrugated roofs mixed with French supermarkets, roundabout sculptures and concrete apartment blocks around Fort-de-France.
MQ.nature: The forested cone of Mount Pelee dominates the north, banana plantations cover the middle slopes with bunches wrapped in blue plastic bags, and the south is drier with sugar cane and scrub.
MQ.extra: Euro prices and French chain stores. The blue banana bags and the French-standard roads together separate Martinique and Guadeloupe from the surrounding Anglophone islands.

MR.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are in Arabic and French, and the main routes are long tarmac ribbons across open desert with sand blowing over the edges and few markings.
MR.built: Flat-roofed sand-coloured concrete buildings, often with Moorish arched windows and decorative ironwork, with tents and scrap-and-cloth shanties on the edge of Nouakchott.
MR.nature: Sand in every direction, pale beige to orange dunes, bare stony hamada, scattered thorn trees, and the grey Atlantic along the western edge.
MR.extra: Sand drifted across the tarmac and windblown blue plastic bags caught on thorn bushes are almost constant.

MS.roads: Drives on the left. Steep narrow sealed roads with British-style signage serve the north, while the entire southern half of the island is an exclusion zone where roads are abandoned and buried under ash.
MS.poles: Wooden poles on the northern roads, with lines running through thick vegetation.
MS.built: Small concrete and timber houses with metal roofs and newly built government offices in the north; in the south, the roofless, ash-buried ruins of Plymouth.
MS.nature: Very green forested volcanic hills in the north, and to the south grey pyroclastic ash fans, dead grey tree trunks and the steaming Soufriere Hills dome.
MS.extra: Volcano hazard zone boundary signs and the observatory. Traffic is extremely light because the population is only a few thousand.

MT.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and M and black characters, usually three letters and three digits.
MT.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Roads are narrow, heavily patched and often bordered by rubble stone walls rather than verges; markings are white with yellow box junctions and kerb restrictions.
MT.poles: Concrete and steel poles carry a lot of visible overhead cable, much of it strung between building parapets in the towns.
MT.built: Almost everything is built from honey-coloured globigerina limestone, with flat roofs crowded with water tanks, aerials and solar panels. Enclosed timber or aluminium balconies painted in strong greens, reds and blues project over the street.
MT.nature: Effectively treeless and very dry, with small terraced fields divided by limestone rubble walls, prickly pear, carob and pale stony ground.
MT.extra: Maltese is written in Latin script but uses ħ, ż and ġ and sounds Arabic, which is unique in Europe. Corner niches with religious statues, red British-pattern post boxes and English-language signage are all common; domains end in .mt.

MU.plates: Reflective white front plates and yellow rear plates with black characters, in the British style.
MU.roads: Drives on the left. British-style markings and English signage, a modern motorway spine with crash barriers, and narrow lanes with raised concrete kerbs winding through sugar cane.
MU.poles: Square-section concrete poles along most roads, with steel lighting columns on the motorway.
MU.built: Flat-roofed concrete houses with rebar left standing for a future floor, bright render, creole timber houses with verandas, and Hindu temples, mosques and churches within sight of each other.
MU.nature: Endless bright green sugar cane, black basalt boulders stacked into piles and walls at the field edges, mango and banyan trees, and jagged volcanic peaks over dark red-brown soil.
MU.extra: Colourful Hindu statues and small roadside shrines, and shop signs mixing French, English and Indian languages.

MV.plates: Small white plates with black characters; motorcycles vastly outnumber cars and most plates seen are motorcycle-sized.
MV.roads: Drives on the left. Roads are short, narrow and mostly unmarked, surfaced in concrete, paving block or bare coral sand, with kerbs and planters instead of guardrail.
MV.poles: Concrete and steel poles carrying local distribution cable on the larger islands.
MV.built: Densely packed concrete blocks of five to ten storeys in Malé with narrow shaded streets, and low rendered or coral-stone houses with corrugated roofs and painted walls on the outer islands.
MV.nature: Coconut palms, screwpine and breadfruit over brilliant white coral sand, with turquoise lagoon water visible almost everywhere and no relief whatsoever.
MV.extra: The round, looping Thaana script running right to left on shop and street signs is unmistakable. Scooters, bicycles and small vans make up nearly all traffic.

MW.plates: White reflective plates with black characters.
MW.roads: Drives on the left. The M1 is narrow tarmac with a white centre line and yellow edge lines and no hard shoulder, crowded with pedestrians and cyclists, with many painted speed humps.
MW.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms along most roads, with concrete poles in Lilongwe and Blantyre.
MW.built: Red fired-brick houses with thatch or corrugated iron roofs, home-made brick kilns standing beside the road, and low commercial strips covered in painted advertising.
MW.nature: Red-brown soil, miombo woodland and very large numbers of mango trees, maize planted right up to the tarmac, and the blue expanse of Lake Malawi to the east.
MW.extra: Bicycle taxis with padded rear seats work every roadside, and Airtel red paint covers shops and kiosks.

MX.plates: Plates are issued per state and print the state name across the top, usually in colour and often with a state graphic or landmark; formats are typically three letters with three or four digits.
MX.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Lines separating opposing traffic are frequently white rather than yellow, a strong contrast with the United States, although newer roads increasingly use yellow. Stop signs read ALTO, warning signs are yellow diamonds, and signed topes speed bumps are extremely common.
MX.poles: Square and round concrete poles are very common in cities and along highways, with wooden poles frequent in rural areas; CFE distribution gear is mounted on the poles.
MX.built: Painted concrete and brick with flat roofs carrying black plastic tinaco water tanks and gas cylinders; colonial centres with arcaded plazas, stone churches and clay tile roofs.
MX.nature: Cactus, mesquite and creosote scrub over pale dusty soil in the north, pine and oak forest and blue agave fields in the centre, and tropical forest and palms in the south and Yucatan.
MX.extra: Spanish signage; OXXO convenience stores are ubiquitous, roadside taquerias and stalls line the highways, and .mx or .com.mx addresses appear on shopfronts.

MY.plates: Black plates with white characters, typically three letters and up to four digits with no state name. Front and rear are identical.
MY.roads: Drives on the left. Expressway signs are green with white text and federal road signs blue, with Jawi Arabic script frequently placed above or below the Latin on street name and town signs; edge lines are white and centre lines yellow where overtaking is banned.
MY.poles: Square and round concrete poles along most roads, with tall steel lattice transmission towers crossing plantations.
MY.built: Rows of two- and three-storey shophouses with covered five-foot walkways, terraced suburban houses with zinc or tiled roofs, and stilted timber kampung houses in villages.
MY.nature: Endless regimented oil palm plantations are the single strongest tell, alongside rubber, dense rainforest edges and bright orange-red lateritic soil cuttings.
MY.extra: Proton and Perodua cars make up much of the traffic. Roadside stalls under blue tarpaulins, mosques with domes, and speed-camera warning signs are common.

MZ.plates: White plates with black characters ending in a two-letter province code, such as MP for Maputo.
MZ.roads: Drives on the left. The EN1 is narrow tarmac with a white centre line and yellow edge markings in places, long single-lane bridge sections, and Portuguese-language signage.
MZ.poles: Concrete poles along the main roads and wooden poles in rural areas, with tall lattice transmission pylons in places.
MZ.built: Pastel-rendered Portuguese colonial buildings with arcades in the old town centres, reed and thatch huts near the coast, and concrete block with corrugated iron elsewhere.
MZ.nature: Huge coconut plantations along the coast, cashew and mango trees, pale sandy soil near the sea turning red-brown inland, and dry miombo woodland.
MZ.extra: Chapa minibuses packed to the doors, sacks of charcoal and cashews for sale on the verges, and Vodacom red branding on kiosks.

NA.plates: White plates with black characters, the letter N then digits then a letter indicating the registering town, such as W for Windhoek.
NA.roads: Drives on the left. Tarmac trunk roads have a white centre line and yellow edge lines, and thousands of kilometres of graded gravel roads run pale grey or deep red with warning signs for loose sand.
NA.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms are the norm, with distinctive tall steel lattice pylons on the main transmission lines.
NA.built: German colonial architecture with steep roofs and gables in Swakopmund and Luderitz, otherwise low flat or shallow-pitched buildings in beige render with corrugated roofs and wide dusty forecourts.
NA.nature: Red Kalahari sand in the east, pale grey gravel plains and bare rock in the west, camelthorn acacia, quiver trees in the south and mopane in the north.
NA.extra: Extremely long empty roads under a low flat horizon, game warning signs, and isolated filling stations carrying South African fuel brands.

NC.plates: White plates with black characters and no EU strip.
NC.roads: Drives on the right. French road signage and markings throughout, with a well-built express dual carriageway around Noumea and long straight sealed roads running down the west coast.
NC.poles: Concrete poles beside the main roads across open savanna.
NC.built: Noumea looks like a French provincial town with pastel apartment blocks, roundabouts and supermarkets, while Kanak tribal areas have round huts with tall conical thatched roofs and carved doorposts.
NC.nature: Columnar Cook pines standing like dark spikes along ridgelines and beaches, red laterite soil, niaouli savanna on the dry west coast and dense rainforest on the wet east.
NC.extra: Terraced red-earth nickel mine scars high on the hillsides are a strong giveaway, as is French signage with CFP franc prices in a Melanesian setting.

NE.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are in French, and the main routes are a single strip of tarmac across flat scrub with sand encroaching at the edges and few markings.
NE.built: Flat-roofed mud-brick houses the same beige as the ground, Hausa-style mosques with wooden spikes protruding from the mud walls, and concrete block buildings in Niamey.
NE.nature: Pale sandy beige soil, sparse acacia and doum palms, flat Sahelian scrub grading into dunes and bare rock towards the Air and Tenere.
NE.extra: Very heavy motorcycle and donkey-cart traffic, and a persistent dusty haze in the air for much of the year.

NF.plates: Plates carrying the name Norfolk Island, usually with a Norfolk pine graphic.
NF.roads: Drives on the left with a 50 kilometres per hour maximum. Cattle have right of way and wander loose on the open roads, and cattle grids are frequent.
NF.poles: Wooden poles along the roads, with pines towering over them.
NF.built: Georgian convict-era stone buildings with white sash windows and shingled roofs at Kingston, and weatherboard bungalows with corrugated metal roofs elsewhere.
NF.nature: Tall, slender, symmetrical Norfolk Island pines silhouetted along every ridge and roadside, rolling green pasture, and basalt cliffs at the coast.
NF.extra: Australian-style road signage in English with Norfuk place names. Free-roaming cows standing in the road are the single most reliable cue.

NG.plates: White plates with black characters and a green strip, carrying the state name and its slogan along the bottom, such as Lagos Centre of Excellence. Format is three letters, three digits and two letters.
NG.roads: Drives on the right. Expressways are wide dual carriageways with faded white markings and concrete median barriers, kerbs painted black-and-white or yellow-and-black, and frequent potholes and police checkpoints.
NG.poles: Square concrete poles in the cities and wooden poles in rural areas, with conspicuous tangles of overhead cable in the towns.
NG.built: Unrendered grey blockwork and concrete frames under rust-brown corrugated iron, high compound walls topped with broken glass or razor wire, and shipping-container shops.
NG.nature: Deep red-orange laterite soil, oil palm and dense green bush in the south, savanna with baobab and locust bean in the north, and a burnt-orange harmattan haze in winter.
NG.extra: Yellow danfo minibuses and keke tricycles in Lagos, MTN yellow and Glo green paint on nearly every kiosk, and hand-painted church signs lining the highways.

NI.plates: White plates with black characters and a blue band reading NICARAGUA with the flag; a leading letter identifies the department of registration, such as M for Managua.
NI.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edges on paved highways, but the distinctive Nicaraguan feature is widespread adoquines, interlocking hexagonal concrete paving blocks, on secondary and town roads.
NI.poles: Square-section concrete poles and wooden poles both occur, with dense low-hanging cable in urban areas.
NI.built: Single-storey buildings hard against the pavement with clay tile or zinc roofs, barred windows and painted render; Leon and Granada have deep colonial arcades and strongly coloured facades.
NI.nature: A chain of volcanic cones along the Pacific side with dry deciduous forest that browns off in the dry season, cattle pasture, and humid green forest towards the Caribbean coast.
NI.extra: Spanish signage; government billboards in Sandinista pink and black, horse-drawn carts on rural roads, and tall steel Arbol de la Vida sculptures around Managua.

NL.plates: Yellow plate front and rear with black characters and a blue EU strip with NL.
NL.roads: Separate cycle tracks surfaced in red asphalt run alongside almost every road and are the fastest tell. Motorway signs are blue, markings white with chunky dashes, and many village streets are paved in brick setts rather than asphalt.
NL.poles: Overhead distribution is essentially absent; power runs underground and only slim lighting columns and tall lattice transmission pylons break the skyline.
NL.built: Dark red and brown brick used for nearly everything, in long terraces with large uncurtained ground-floor windows, white-painted frames and stepped or bell gables in older centres.
NL.nature: Dead flat polder landscape ruled into rectangles by drainage ditches and canals, with pollarded willows, poplar rows and grazing dairy cattle. No natural hills at all.
NL.extra: Blue-and-white street name signs are usually fixed to building walls rather than posts. Lift bridges, dykes and pumping stations are frequent, and domains end in .nl.

NO.plates: White plate with a blue strip and N on the left and black characters, two letters and five digits.
NO.roads: Centre lines are yellow while edge lines are white, which separates Norway instantly from Sweden and Finland. Warning triangles have a yellow background, direction signs to local destinations are yellow with black text while major routes are blue, and tunnels are extremely frequent.
NO.poles: Creosoted wooden poles carry rural distribution, often climbing straight up steep slopes.
NO.built: Timber houses with horizontal weatherboarding painted deep red, white, ochre or grey, with white trim and steep roofs; some older buildings keep grass turf roofs. Coastal villages line the water on stilted wooden quays.
NO.nature: Deep fjords, bare glacier-scoured granite, spruce and pine at lower levels giving way to stunted birch and open fell higher up, and countless waterfalls.
NO.extra: Norwegian uses æ, ø and å. Automatic toll gantries marked AutoPASS span the main roads, and road numbers are prefixed E, Fv or Rv; domains end in .no.

NP.plates: Private vehicles carry red plates with white Devanagari characters, a distinctive and quick identifier; public transport uses black plates with white characters and other categories use green or yellow.
NP.roads: Drives on the left. Narrow mountain roads with broken or absent markings, low whitewashed stone kerbs and posts, frequent landslide scars, and blue or green signs in Devanagari above English.
NP.poles: Concrete and steel poles carrying dense untidy cable bundles, particularly extreme in Kathmandu where wiring hangs in thick loops.
NP.built: Narrow multi-storey brick and concrete buildings with flat roofs and exposed rebar, older red brick houses with carved dark timber windows, and tiered pagoda temples with brass finials.
NP.nature: Steeply terraced green hillsides, subtropical sal forest and banana in the Terai lowlands, rhododendron and pine higher up, with white Himalayan peaks on the skyline.
NP.extra: Heavily decorated Tata trucks and buses, strings of prayer flags, and painted eyes on Buddhist stupas. Dust and haze in the valleys is very characteristic.

NR.roads: Drives on the left. A single sealed ring road of about 19 kilometres circles the island close to the shore, mostly unmarked, with a spur climbing to the interior plateau.
NR.poles: Concrete poles along the coastal ring road carrying a simple line of cable.
NR.built: Low concrete buildings with metal roofs strung along the coastal strip, plus large areas of rusting phosphate industrial plant, conveyors and the cantilever loaders at Aiwo.
NR.nature: A narrow fringe of coconut palms and coastal scrub, with the interior Topside a moonscape of bare grey coral limestone pinnacles left by phosphate mining.
NR.extra: The airport runway runs alongside the ring road, and abandoned mining machinery rusts in the open almost everywhere.

NU.roads: Drives on the left. A single sealed ring road circles a small raised coral island with almost no traffic and no lane markings, with numbered sea tracks branching off towards the coast.
NU.poles: Wooden and concrete poles following the ring road.
NU.built: Scattered concrete houses with metal roofs, many of them empty and overgrown because of emigration, plus whitewashed churches and a small cluster of government buildings at Alofi.
NU.nature: Dense low coastal forest growing straight out of jagged grey raised coral makatea, coconut palms, and sheer limestone cliffs at the shore rather than beaches.
NU.extra: New Zealand dollars and New Zealand-style road signs. The unusually high proportion of abandoned, vine-covered houses is itself a tell.

NZ.plates: White or occasionally black plates with black characters, no country strip. Format is three letters then three digits.
NZ.roads: Drives on the left. White centre lines, yellow no-overtaking lines, and very frequent one-lane bridges with give-way signs in rural areas.
NZ.poles: Wooden poles predominate, often weathered grey, with distinctive orange-brown crossarms in places.
NZ.built: Single-storey timber houses with corrugated steel roofs, wide eaves and often a verandah.
NZ.nature: Tree ferns, cabbage trees, tussock grass on the high country, and radiata pine plantations in blocks.
NZ.extra: Route markers are a red shield for state highways. Sheep fencing with wooden battens is everywhere.
