OM.plates: White plates with black digits and a letter code, with the country name in Arabic and English; taxi plates and vehicles are marked in orange.
OM.roads: Drives on the right. Excellent wide asphalt with crisp white markings, brown tourist signs and green and blue direction signs in Arabic above English, and heavy grey guardrail on wadi crossings.
OM.poles: Galvanised steel and concrete poles along rural roads, with lattice transmission towers crossing the gravel plains.
OM.built: Low white and sand-coloured buildings in a mandated traditional style, with crenellated parapets, arched windows and decorative merlons, plus restored mud-brick forts and watchtowers on hilltops.
OM.nature: Jagged bare brown and near-black rock mountains, gravel plains, and sudden dense date palm oases with falaj irrigation channels in the wadis.
OM.extra: Orange-and-white taxis are a fast confirmation. Traffic is dominated by white Toyota Land Cruisers and pickups, and speed bumps appear even on rural roads.

PA.plates: White plates with black characters, usually two letters and four digits, with PANAMA and the year of validity printed on the plate.
PA.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edges, with the Pan-American Highway and the Corredor motorways in good condition, concrete barriers and overhead sign gantries around Panama City.
PA.poles: Round and square concrete poles are common on main roads, with wooden poles in rural districts.
PA.built: Concrete block houses with zinc roofs and barred windows in towns, a dense wall of glass high-rise towers in Panama City, and Caribbean-style timber buildings in Colon and Bocas del Toro.
PA.nature: Humid tropical forest with tall canopy trees, oil palm and banana plantations, cleared rolling cattle pasture in the Azuero, and mangrove along both coasts.
PA.extra: Spanish signage but US dollars in circulation as the balboa. Canal and shipping infrastructure is visible on the central corridor, and .pa or .com.pa addresses appear on shopfronts.

PE.plates: White plates with black characters in a three letter, dash, three digit format, with a small red and white national strip.
PE.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edge lines, with black-and-white painted kerbs, gabion and stone retaining walls on mountain roads, and frequent toll plazas on the Pan-American Highway.
PE.poles: Round concrete poles with a tapering profile are widespread in cities and along the coast; wooden poles appear in the Andes and the jungle.
PE.built: Unrendered red brick and concrete houses with flat roofs, protruding rebar and rooftop water tanks, packed onto steep hillsides; adobe with clay tile roofs in Andean villages.
PE.nature: A completely barren grey-brown sand and rock desert runs the whole coast, cut by sharply irrigated green river valleys; high treeless puna and snow peaks in the Andes and dense rainforest in the east.
PE.extra: Spanish signage, with political party names and candidate slogans painted directly onto house walls and rock faces, a very reliable Peruvian cue. Three-wheeled mototaxis dominate small-town traffic.

PF.plates: White plates with black characters and no EU strip, unlike metropolitan France.
PF.roads: Drives on the right. Tahiti has a short dual carriageway around Papeete and otherwise a two-lane sealed coast road, marked at intervals by concrete PK kilometre-point posts, which is a very reliable tell.
PF.poles: Concrete poles follow the coast road closely, with the sea on one side and the mountain wall on the other.
PF.built: Single-storey houses with metal roofs and wide verandahs painted in strong colours, Catholic and Protestant churches in each village, and roulotte food vans on the waterfront in Papeete.
PF.nature: Sheer green volcanic spires and knife ridges on the Society Islands, breadfruit and mape chestnut trees, coconut palms and a barrier reef line offshore; the Tuamotus are flat coral atolls.
PF.extra: French signage with Tahitian place names and CFP franc prices. Tiare flowers worn behind the ear and outrigger canoes pulled up on the shore.

PG.plates: White plates with black characters in a letters-then-digits layout.
PG.roads: Drives on the left. The Highlands Highway is the main sealed artery and is often potholed and unmarked, with people walking along both verges in large numbers; most other roads are unsealed and badly rutted.
PG.poles: Wooden and concrete poles along the highway, with long unserved sections and frequent small diesel generators instead.
PG.built: Corrugated-iron and rough timber buildings, with commercial premises in towns behind high security fences topped with razor wire and manned gates; villages have thatched houses with steep gables.
PG.nature: Pale kunai grass on the highland slopes with casuarina windbreaks and coffee gardens, and dense dark lowland rainforest at low altitude.
PG.extra: Very high pedestrian density along rural roads, crowded PMV minibuses and open-backed trucks, roadside betel nut stalls and red betel spit stains on the tarmac.

PH.plates: White plates with black characters, usually three letters and four digits, with the country name at the top; older plates use green characters on white.
PH.roads: Drives on the right, which separates it sharply from most of maritime South-East Asia. Signs are green with white text on expressways and white or blue elsewhere, all in English, and concrete rather than asphalt carriageways are very common.
PH.poles: Round concrete and tall timber poles carrying very heavy cable bundles and drum transformers, with characteristic slack looping spans.
PH.built: Concrete hollow-block houses with corrugated galvanised iron roofs painted red, green or left rusting, plus timber and bamboo houses in rural barangays.
PH.nature: Coconut palms everywhere, banana, mango, rice paddy, and steep green volcanic hills with red-brown soil.
PH.extra: An outdoor basketball court in practically every barangay is the single most reliable giveaway, along with jeepneys, motorbike tricycles with side cars, small sari-sari shops behind grilles, and roadside Catholic shrines.

PK.plates: White plates with black characters for private vehicles and yellow with black for commercial ones, but designs vary by province and many older hand-painted plates with Urdu lettering remain.
PK.roads: Drives on the left. Motorway signs are green with white text and other signs blue or white in Urdu and English; kerbs and roadside trees are painted in black-and-white bands and median barriers are low concrete.
PK.poles: Concrete poles of square section and steel lattice masts, carrying heavy tangled cable bundles in towns.
PK.built: Fired brick is the dominant material, in plain brick walls or rendered and painted, with flat roofs, parapets, and rolling shutters on shopfronts; brick kiln chimneys punctuate the plains.
PK.nature: Flat irrigated plains of wheat, rice, sugarcane and cotton with eucalyptus and shisham lines, dry scrub and desert in the south-west, and bare high mountains in the north.
PK.extra: Elaborately decorated jingle trucks and buses covered in painted panels, mirror work and hanging chains are the outstanding tell. Small Suzuki Mehran cars, Bolan vans and motorbike rickshaws fill the roads.

PL.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and PL and black characters; the first one to three letters identify the voivodeship and district, followed by a mixed group of digits and letters.
PL.roads: Warning signs have a yellow background, which is a quick tell. Markings are white, and rural roads commonly have narrow or no shoulders with a mown grass verge and a shallow ditch.
PL.poles: Slim tapered grey concrete poles are standard, frequently paired or braced with a lattice-like frame near the base on rural low-voltage lines.
PL.built: Rendered houses in white and pastel shades with steep tiled roofs and enclosed porches, socialist-era blocks on town edges, red-brick Gothic churches in the north, and log-built cottages in the east and south.
PL.nature: Flat to gently rolling country with extensive pine plantations, birch, pale sandy soil, and fields divided into long narrow strips that create a striped pattern across the landscape.
PL.extra: Polish uses ł, ż, ź, ę, ą, ś, ć and ń. Small roadside shrines and crucifixes hung with flowers appear at village entrances and field corners, and domains end in .pl.

PM.plates: French-style white plates with black characters.
PM.roads: Drives on the right, with full French road signage and markings, European sign shapes and distances in kilometres, just off the coast of Newfoundland. Streets are narrow and often lined with snow banks.
PM.poles: Wooden poles with North American style cabling and transformers.
PM.built: Tightly packed timber houses painted in strong reds, blues and yellows with steep roofs to shed snow, a large French church, and French municipal buildings.
PM.nature: Treeless or scrubby barrens, low rocky hills, stunted conifers bent by the wind, frequent fog and a cold grey Atlantic.
PM.extra: Renault, Peugeot and Citroen cars on North American-looking streets is the single strongest giveaway, along with euro prices and the French tricolour.

PN.extra: A single settlement of a few dozen people linked by steep unsealed concrete tracks used almost entirely by quad bikes; there is no conventional road network and essentially no street-level imagery.

PR.plates: US-sized white plates reading Puerto Rico, commonly with the Isla del Encanto slogan and a garita sentry box graphic.
PR.roads: Drives on the right. Distances and route markers are in kilometres while speed limits are posted in miles per hour, a combination found essentially nowhere else. Green American-style direction signs are written in Spanish, and the autopista network has toll gantries.
PR.poles: Heavy concrete utility poles with dense overhead cabling, interspersed with replacement wooden poles and visibly repaired lines after hurricane damage.
PR.built: Flat-roofed concrete houses painted in bright colours, with decorative iron rejas over windows and doors, carports and water cisterns on the roof.
PR.nature: Lush green karst mogote hills in the north, flamboyan trees with vivid red flowers, royal palms, and dry cactus scrub along the south coast.
PR.extra: Spanish-language signage on American road geometry, with US chain stores, US Postal Service boxes and roadside chinchorro food stands.

PS.plates: Palestinian Authority plates are white with green characters and a green band on the left carrying P; Israeli yellow plates also appear on many vehicles in the same areas.
PS.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are green, blue or white with Arabic and English and sometimes Hebrew, markings are worn, and roads are punctuated by concrete blocks, checkpoints and speed bumps.
PS.poles: Concrete and steel poles with dense cable bundles, with many buildings served by informal overhead connections.
PS.built: Pale limestone-clad and rendered concrete blocks with flat roofs, black plastic water tanks and white solar heaters on every roof, and top floors frequently left unfinished with rebar protruding.
PS.nature: Terraced rocky hillsides of olive groves and dry grass with pale limestone outcrops, almond and fig trees, and dusty tan soil.
PS.extra: Black roof water tanks in clusters, political murals and martyr posters on walls, and the grey concrete separation wall with graffiti where it runs near roads.

PT.plates: White plate front and rear with black characters, a blue EU strip with P on the left and a narrow yellow vertical band on the right carrying the month and year of registration. Older plates are yellow at the rear and white at the front.
PT.roads: Motorway direction signs are blue and other roads are signed white on a dark background or black on white. Markings are white, and many pavements are laid as calçada, small black and white limestone and basalt setts in geometric patterns.
PT.poles: Grey concrete poles with a rounded top and a pair of holes through the shaft are very common outside the cities.
PT.built: Azulejo tiled facades in blue, green and yellow, terracotta pantile roofs, and whitewashed walls with a painted blue or ochre band framing doors and windows in the south.
PT.nature: Cork oaks with orange stripped trunks, dense eucalyptus plantations, umbrella pines near the coast, and dry ochre soil inland.
PT.extra: Street name plaques are often glazed ceramic tiles with blue lettering. Talho, Pastelaria and Mercearia appear on shopfronts and domains end in .pt.

PW.plates: US-sized plates carrying the name Palau.
PW.roads: Drives on the right. The Compact Road around Babeldaob is a smooth, well-engineered two-lane sealed road with crisp white edge lines running through empty jungle, oddly high quality for the tiny volume of traffic.
PW.poles: Concrete poles follow the main roads, with long unpoled stretches through the forest.
PW.built: Koror is low-rise painted concrete with metal roofs and shopfront signage; village buildings are modest concrete boxes, with Japanese-era concrete structures surviving in places.
PW.nature: Dense jungle pressing on the road, mangrove channels, and steeply undercut limestone Rock Islands visible offshore from the southern roads.
PW.extra: Traffic is extremely light and the road can be empty for kilometres. American vehicles and dollar pricing sit alongside Japanese and Palauan signage.

PY.plates: Mercosur plates: white with a blue strip across the top reading PARAGUAY. Older plates are plain white with black characters and the city of registration.
PY.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Sealed routes carry white edge lines with markings often worn away, wide red-earth shoulders, and long stretches of unsealed red laterite on secondary roads; towns frequently have cobbled or brick-paved streets.
PY.poles: Wooden poles are common on rural roads with square and round concrete poles in towns, and long runs of slim poles follow the highways across open country.
PY.built: Single-storey houses with wide verandas, brick walls and clay tile or corrugated roofs, much of it left as unrendered red brick; village shops open straight onto red dirt streets.
PY.nature: Deep red laterite soil is the strongest visual cue, with green rolling farmland, soy and cattle in the east, and flat grey-green thorn scrub and palm savanna in the Chaco.
PY.extra: Spanish signage with widespread Guarani on shops and place names, which is unique in the region. Heavy motorcycle traffic, roadside chipa sellers, and Brazilian goods in the border towns.

QA.plates: White plates with black digits only and no letters, with the country name in Arabic and English across the top. Numbers are often very short.
QA.roads: Drives on the right. Extremely wide, smooth multi-lane roads with green and blue direction signs in Arabic above English, heavy use of concrete barriers, and large signalised interchanges replacing older roundabouts.
QA.built: Sand-coloured rendered villas with flat roofs behind high walls, arranged in grid blocks, with a dense cluster of glass towers on the Doha skyline.
QA.nature: Flat pale gravel and sand desert with almost no natural vegetation; all roadside greenery is irrigated planting with visible black drip lines.
QA.extra: Turquoise Karwa taxis are a quick confirmation. Verges are immaculately raked, and construction hoarding and sand drift are a constant presence.

RE.plates: French plates: white with black characters, a blue EU strip with F, and the department number 974 in the right-hand band.
RE.roads: Drives on the right. The coastal Route du Littoral is a four-lane road squeezed under overhanging cliffs with rockfall netting, alongside the new elevated viaduct built out over the sea, while inland roads climb in tight hairpins into the cirques.
RE.poles: Concrete poles along the coastal and mid-slope roads.
RE.built: Creole houses with ornate lambrequin fretwork and bright paintwork, alongside French apartment blocks, supermarkets and roundabouts in Saint-Denis and Saint-Pierre.
RE.nature: Sugar cane blanketing the coastal slopes, tree ferns and tamarin forest higher up, and black basalt lava flows crossing the road at Le Grand Brule in the south-east.
RE.extra: Euro prices and French signage in the Indian Ocean, with shark warning notices on the beaches and the volcano road up to Piton de la Fournaise.

RO.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and RO; the county code of one or two letters is followed by two digits and three letters. Bucharest plates start with B.
RO.roads: National roads are frequently lined with continuous avenues of poplar or walnut trees and the trunks are whitewashed to head height. Markings are white and often worn, shoulders are narrow, and horse-drawn carts with a red reflective triangle still share rural routes.
RO.poles: Grey concrete poles, many rectangular in section with a vertical row of holes, carry most distribution; wooden poles survive on village spurs.
RO.built: Rural houses with elaborate pressed-metal or carved timber porches and gates painted blue or green, under terracotta or corrugated metal roofs. Transylvanian villages have Saxon fortified churches and long street-facing gable walls; towns are ringed with grey socialist blocks.
RO.nature: Beech and spruce on the Carpathians, wide plains of maize and sunflower, and hay stacked in tall conical ricks around a central pole, which is a strong regional marker.
RO.extra: Romanian is a Romance language in Latin script using ș, ț, ă and î, so it reads oddly familiar amid Slavic neighbours. Tall wooden crucifixes stand at crossroads, Non Stop shop signs are ubiquitous and domains end in .ro.

RS.plates: White plate with a blue strip and SRB on the left; the town code appears in Latin with a smaller Cyrillic version printed above it, then a small coat of arms, then digits and two letters.
RS.roads: Motorway direction signs are green and other main roads blue. Markings are white, main corridors are well surfaced while local roads are patched, and kerbs and tree bases are often whitewashed.
RS.poles: Grey concrete poles, square or round, carry most rural distribution, with heavy cable bundles in towns.
RS.built: Unfinished houses in red brick within concrete frames are common, under red pantile roofs. Vojvodina has low Austro-Hungarian street facades in pastel render, while Belgrade mixes nineteenth-century blocks with large socialist estates.
RS.nature: Flat black-soil plains of maize and sunflower in the north broken by poplar windbreaks, wooded rolling hills in the centre and south.
RS.extra: Cyrillic and Latin frequently appear on the same sign, and a lot of shop signage is Latin only. Pekara, Mesara and Roštilj signs are constant; domains end in .rs.

RU.plates: White plate with black characters in a letter, three digits, two letters pattern, and a small panel on the right-hand end showing the region number above a tiny tricolour and the letters RUS. The country marking on the right rather than the left is the tell.
RU.roads: Direction signs are green on motorway-grade routes and blue elsewhere. Markings are white, shoulders are often unsealed, and delineator posts are white with a black top and red reflector.
RU.poles: Round tapered spun-concrete poles and square concrete posts dominate; villages often use short wooden poles spliced onto concrete stubs.
RU.built: Soviet panel and brick apartment blocks in every town, and single-storey timber village houses with ornately carved and painted window surrounds in blue, white and green under corrugated or slate roofs. Orthodox churches carry onion domes in gold or blue.
RU.nature: Birch stands with distinctive white trunks, dark taiga spruce and pine, immense flat plains, and open grass steppe with black soil in the south.
RU.extra: All signage is Cyrillic, with Latin transliteration on major routes. Concrete bus shelters with mosaic panels, АЗС fuel stations and Магазин shopfronts are everywhere; domains end in .ru.

RW.plates: White plates with black characters beginning RA plus a letter, then three digits and a letter; government vehicles use a GR series.
RW.roads: Drives on the right. The tarmac is unusually smooth and well-marked for the region, with white lines, painted black-and-white kerbstones, concrete drainage channels and armco on the hairpins.
RW.poles: Slim round concrete poles, evenly spaced and noticeably upright, with regular street lighting along main roads.
RW.built: Brick and rendered houses with clay-tile or corrugated iron roofs on terraced hillsides, tidy planned villages, and modern glass buildings in central Kigali.
RW.nature: Steep green hills terraced to the summit with banana, tea and eucalyptus, deep red-brown soil, and almost no uncultivated land.
RW.extra: Motorcycle taxi riders wear numbered vests and helmets, there is no plastic bag litter anywhere, and verges are mown with planted hedges.

SA.plates: White plates with black characters laid out with Arabic letters and numerals on one side and their Latin and Western-numeral equivalents mirrored alongside, a distinctive dual-script arrangement.
SA.roads: Drives on the right. Very wide highways with green direction signs in Arabic above English, white markings, long runs of grey guardrail, and camel warning signs in rural areas.
SA.poles: Steel lattice and tubular steel poles along highways, with concrete poles in towns; long transmission lines cross open desert.
SA.built: Sand and beige rendered concrete with flat roofs, high perimeter walls and roof water tanks, with mosques and minarets at frequent intervals and older mud-brick ruins nearby.
SA.nature: Gravel and sand desert with acacia scrub, deep red-orange dunes in the Nafud and Empty Quarter, dark volcanic lava fields in the west, and green terraced mountains in Asir.
SA.extra: Sand drift across the carriageway, camels beside fences, and traffic dominated by white Toyota pickups and large SUVs. Petrol stations with mosques attached appear at regular intervals.

SB.roads: Drives on the left. Honiara's Kukum Highway is sealed and kerbed, but outside town the roads are unsealed coral or mud, deeply potholed, with rivers crossed by shallow fords rather than bridges.
SB.poles: Wooden and concrete poles in and around Honiara, with sagging lines; essentially none on the outer islands.
SB.built: Timber and leaf houses raised on posts with corrugated-iron roofs, plus rows of tin-roofed Chinatown shophouses in Honiara and simple concrete stores.
SB.nature: Dense rainforest right to the road edge, coconut and oil palm plantations in regular rows, steep green ridges and brown river deltas.
SB.extra: Second World War relics and memorials appear along the roads around Honiara and on Guadalcanal, and betel nut stalls line the verges.

SC.plates: White front and yellow rear plates with black characters, the registration beginning with the letter S.
SC.roads: Drives on the left. Very narrow steep tarmac lanes with white lines and low concrete kerbs, crash barriers above the sea cliffs, and English signage.
SC.poles: Concrete poles along the coast roads, with lines strung tight against steep slopes.
SC.built: Creole houses with steep corrugated or tiled roofs and verandas, modern concrete villas terraced into the hillsides, and small painted shops at the roadside.
SC.nature: Huge rounded grey granite boulders, dense green jungle, coconut and takamaka trees, and white sand against turquoise water.
SC.extra: The granite boulders on the beaches are the giveaway, and roads hug the shoreline with steep forested hills rising immediately inland.

SD.roads: Drives on the right. Signage is in Arabic with some English, and the main highways are long straight tarmac across desert with sand drifting across the edges.
SD.built: Flat-roofed mud-brick and concrete buildings in sand and ochre tones, with small deep-set windows and a fine layer of dust over everything.
SD.nature: Sand and stony desert across the north, a narrow green ribbon of date palms and irrigated fields along the Nile, and thorn scrub savanna further south.

SE.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and S and black characters, three letters followed by three digits or two digits and a letter.
SE.roads: Warning triangles have a yellow background. Centre lines are white, unlike Norway, and many main roads are 2+1 layouts split by a steel wire-rope barrier on slim posts, which is a strong Swedish tell.
SE.poles: Creosoted wooden poles carry most rural distribution, often running along the forest edge.
SE.built: Timber houses painted Falu red with white corners and window frames, plus yellow or grey rendered buildings and standing-seam metal roofs. Modern housing is low, pale and set among trees.
SE.nature: Endless pine and spruce forest with birch, rounded granite outcrops and boulders, many lakes, and open rapeseed and wheat plains in the far south.
SE.extra: Swedish uses å, ä and ö and street names end in -gatan or -vägen. Elk warning signs are frequent, reflector posts line the verges, and domains end in .se.

SG.plates: Front plates are white with black characters and rear plates yellow with black, the pairing being a quick identifier; older vehicles carry black plates with white characters.
SG.roads: Drives on the left. Immaculate asphalt with perfectly crisp white and yellow markings, green expressway signs, and chevron-marked road edges; kerbs are painted with yellow or red-and-white bands to indicate parking restrictions.
SG.poles: Almost all cabling is underground; street lights are slim galvanised steel columns with a single curved arm.
SG.built: Tall uniform HDB housing blocks with open void decks at ground level dominate, alongside restored colourful shophouses and a dense glass core downtown.
SG.nature: Manicured tropical planting with broad rain trees arching over expressways, angsana, palms and dense secondary forest kept neatly trimmed at the road edge.
SG.extra: Overhead ERP toll gantries, blue-and-white street name signs, and the complete absence of litter, potholes or hand-painted signage set it apart from neighbouring Malaysia.

SH.roads: Drives on the left with a low speed limit. Roads are extremely narrow single-track tarmac with passing places, climbing out of Jamestown in tight hairpins, and drivers sound the horn at blind bends.
SH.poles: Wooden poles along the roads, carrying lines across bare hillsides.
SH.built: Jamestown is a single Georgian street of white and pastel-painted buildings wedged into a narrow bare valley; elsewhere there are small bungalows with metal roofs scattered across the uplands.
SH.nature: Bare brown and grey volcanic slopes and cliffs near the coast rising to green flax-covered uplands with Norfolk pines; Ascension is almost entirely black lava and red cinder cones.
SH.extra: Jacob's Ladder, a straight staircase of nearly 700 steps up the valley side at Jamestown, is unmistakable. British road signs and pillar boxes appear in the middle of the South Atlantic.

SI.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and SLO and, most distinctively, a green border line around the edge; the town code is followed by a small coat of arms, then the registration.
SI.roads: Motorway direction signs are green and other main roads blue. Markings are white and generally crisp, the network is well maintained, and a windscreen vignette is required for motorways.
SI.poles: Concrete and wooden poles both appear on rural lines; distribution is buried in most towns.
SI.built: Alpine-influenced houses with wide eaves, timber balconies and shallow roofs in the north, Mediterranean pantiles and stone in the south-west. Small white churches with a slim onion-domed spire sit on almost every hilltop.
SI.nature: More than half the country is forest, mostly beech and spruce; limestone karst with sinkholes and caves, sheer Julian Alps peaks, and vineyards on steep terraced slopes.
SI.extra: Tall open-sided wooden hayracks, the kozolec, standing in fields are a distinctive national marker. Slovenian uses č, š and ž and domains end in .si.

SJ.plates: Norwegian-style plates, but Svalbard registrations use the letter pair ZN, which is unique to the archipelago.
SJ.roads: Drives on the right. Longyearbyen has only a few kilometres of road, mostly gravel or snow-packed, ending abruptly against the valley sides, and there are no roads at all between settlements.
SJ.poles: Wooden poles alongside insulated pipelines carried above ground on timber trestles, since nothing can be buried in permafrost.
SJ.built: Rectangular timber buildings painted in strong colours and raised on stilts above the permafrost, with old coal-mine cableway pylons and derelict mine buildings on the slopes above.
SJ.nature: Completely treeless. Bare scree slopes below flat-topped mountains, glaciers filling the valley heads, and snow on the ground for most of the year.
SJ.extra: Polar bear warning signs at the edge of town, rifles carried openly outside the settlement, and rows of snowmobiles parked beside houses. Jan Mayen has only a staffed weather station and no public roads.

SK.plates: White plate with a blue EU strip and SK; the two-letter district code is followed by the national coat of arms, a white double cross on three hills, then three digits and two letters.
SK.roads: Motorway direction signs are green and other main roads blue. Markings are white, delineator posts are white with a black cap, and mountain roads have long stretches of crash barrier and snow poles.
SK.poles: Slim grey concrete poles are typical, similar in form to those in Czechia, with wooden poles on older village lines.
SK.built: Rendered village houses in pale yellow, green and pink with steep tiled roofs, panelák estates on town edges, hilltop castles and ruins, and shingled wooden churches in the east.
SK.nature: Spruce-covered Carpathian ridges rising to bare granite peaks in the High Tatras, vineyards in the west, and flat maize country along the Danube lowland.
SK.extra: Slovak uses ľ, ŕ, ô and ä. Houses often carry two number plaques, one red and one blue, and domains end in .sk.

SL.roads: Drives on the right. Freetown is congested with faded markings, the rebuilt highways are decent tarmac with white lines, and roads upcountry are deep red laterite.
SL.poles: Wooden poles and slim concrete poles, with heavy cable tangles through Freetown.
SL.built: Zinc-roofed board houses and concrete block buildings stacked up Freetown's steep hillsides, some Krio wooden houses with shutters and verandas, and mud-and-wattle huts with thatch upcountry.
SL.nature: Deep red laterite soil, dense green bush with oil palm and mango, forested hills rising straight out of the sea behind Freetown, and standing water and mud in the wet season.
SL.extra: Yellow keke tricycles and okada motorcycle taxis everywhere, with Africell and Orange branding painted on kiosks.

SM.plates: White plate with blue characters, a pale blue strip on the left carrying the three-towers coat of arms and the letters RSM. Blue lettering on white is unique in the region.
SM.roads: Steep two-lane roads climbing the flanks of a single limestone ridge, with white markings, Italian-pattern signage and heavy metal barriers on the drop side. Route numbers are prefixed SS.
SM.built: Italian in character: rendered and stone buildings in cream and ochre with terracotta pantiles and green shutters, medieval towers and walls along the ridge, and modern commercial and light-industrial sprawl on the lower slopes.
SM.nature: Rolling Apennine foothills with oak woodland, cypress, olive and vine, and long views out over the Adriatic plain.
SM.extra: Everything is written in Italian but the national flag and coat of arms appear constantly on signs, lamp posts and shopfronts. Duty-free souvenir, electronics and weapon shops cluster near the tourist routes; domains end in .sm.

SN.plates: White plates with black characters grouped into letters and digits.
SN.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are in French, the Dakar motorway is modern with toll plazas and crash barriers, and elsewhere two-lane tarmac runs between sandy verges with black-and-white painted kerbs.
SN.poles: Square-section concrete poles along main roads, with wooden poles inland.
SN.built: Flat-roofed concrete houses in sand and ochre render, often unfinished with rebar, whitewashed mosques with twin minarets, and French colonial facades in Saint-Louis and central Dakar.
SN.nature: Pale sandy soil with lone baobabs standing in flat millet and groundnut fields, doum palms, and mangrove in the Casamance and Sine-Saloum deltas.
SN.extra: Yellow-and-black Dakar taxis, blue-and-yellow painted minibuses, and horse-drawn carts sharing the tarmac with traffic.

SO.nature: Dry thorn scrub over pale sandy and stony ground, frankincense and acacia in the northern hills, and a long white-sand coastline with low dunes.

SR.plates: White plates with black characters and a leading letter coding the vehicle class.
SR.roads: Traffic drives on the left, one of only two mainland South American countries to do so. Coastal roads are flat and narrow with white markings where present, bordered by drainage canals and dykes inherited from Dutch land management.
SR.poles: Concrete poles are common in Paramaribo, with wooden poles along the coastal roads.
SR.built: Dutch colonial timber buildings painted white with green shutters and steep roofs in Paramaribo; elsewhere simple houses raised on posts with corrugated zinc roofs.
SR.nature: A narrow flat coastal plain of rice paddy, cane and mangrove backed by an unbroken wall of rainforest inland, with no relief near the populated strip.
SR.extra: Dutch signage, with straat and weg in street names, is unique in the Americas. Hindu mandirs with jhandi flags, mosques and Javanese villages reflect the population, and right-hand-drive Japanese imports are the norm.

SS.nature: Flat green savanna and vast seasonal swamp along the Nile, with dark cracked clay soil and scattered acacia and doum palms.

ST.roads: Drives on the right. A single narrow coastal ring road with broken tarmac, almost no markings, and Portuguese signage.
ST.built: Faded Portuguese colonial roca plantation buildings with arcades and tiled roofs, alongside timber houses raised on short stilts with corrugated iron roofs.
ST.nature: Dense wet rainforest with cocoa and oil palm, black volcanic sand beaches, and sheer forested volcanic pinnacles inland.

SV.plates: White plates with blue or black characters and a leading class letter, P for private, with EL SALVADOR printed on the plate.
SV.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow centre lines and white edges on the main highways, narrow shoulders, heavy speed bumps, and black-and-white painted kerbs and tree trunks in towns.
SV.poles: Square-section concrete poles are very common, alongside round concrete and some wooden poles, carrying dense low-slung wiring.
SV.built: Concrete block and brick houses with corrugated metal or clay tile roofs, high perimeter walls topped with razor wire or broken glass, and heavy window bars even on small shops.
SV.nature: Volcanic cones and dark fertile soil, coffee on the upper slopes, sugar cane and maize on the plains, and dry deciduous forest near the Pacific.
SV.extra: Spanish signage and US dollar prices. Former American school buses repainted as brightly decorated public buses are everywhere, and .sv addresses appear on shopfronts.

SX.plates: Plates carrying the island name St Maarten.
SX.roads: Drives on the right. Congested two-lane roads around Philipsburg and Simpson Bay with Dutch-style signage, a lifting bridge over the lagoon entrance, and a road running directly under the approach to the runway at Maho Beach.
SX.poles: Wooden poles carrying dense overhead cabling along the main roads.
SX.built: Front Street in Philipsburg has West Indian timber buildings with gingerbread trim and duty-free shopfronts, with large concrete resorts, casinos and cruise facilities elsewhere.
SX.nature: Dry scrubby hills with cactus and acacia, a large salt pond immediately behind Philipsburg, and white sand beaches.
SX.extra: US dollars are used everywhere despite the Dutch status, and aircraft pass extremely low over the beach on landing.

SY.plates: White plates with black characters and a governorate code, with the country name in Arabic; several older layouts remain in circulation.
SY.roads: Drives on the right. Wide older highways with worn markings, green and blue direction signs in Arabic above English, and frequent checkpoints, earth berms and concrete blocks narrowing the carriageway.
SY.built: Beige concrete and breeze block with flat roofs and rooftop water tanks, dark basalt stone building in the southern Hauran, and extensive shell and collapse damage in many towns.
SY.nature: Olive and pistachio groves and wheat on pale brown soil in the west, dry steppe and gravel desert in the east, and bare limestone hills near the coast.
SY.extra: Imagery is sparse and largely dated. Flags, portraits and militia banners on lamp posts and walls, and older Iranian and Japanese saloons, are the common street furniture.

SZ.plates: White reflective plates with black characters, most carrying the letters SD for the country.
SZ.roads: Drives on the left. Good tarmac with white centre lines and yellow edge lines in the South African style, with armco guardrails on the steep mountain descents.
SZ.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms on rural roads, concrete poles and street lighting in the towns.
SZ.built: Small brick and plastered houses with corrugated or tiled pitched roofs, beehive-shaped thatched huts in traditional homesteads, and low shopping strips carrying South African chain branding.
SZ.nature: Rolling green hills with large pine and eucalyptus plantations, sugar cane on the hot lowveld, bare granite domes, and red-brown soil.
SZ.extra: The country is consistently hilly and unusually well-kept for the region, and South African retail and fuel brands are everywhere.

TC.plates: Plates carrying the words Turks and Caicos Islands.
TC.roads: Drives on the left, although almost every vehicle is a left-hand-drive American import. Providenciales has wide, straight, recently surfaced roads with numerous roundabouts crossing flat scrubland.
TC.poles: Concrete poles on Providenciales and wooden poles on the quieter islands, with lines running over low bush.
TC.built: Low-rise pastel resorts and white-walled villas with shallow roofs along the beaches, simple concrete houses in the settlements, and a lot of active construction.
TC.nature: Extremely flat and dry, with silver-grey low scrub, sea grape and casuarina, white salt flats and brilliant pale turquoise shallows offshore.
TC.extra: US dollars, American cars and American supermarkets combined with left-hand traffic and British-style road signs.

TD.nature: Pale sandy Sahelian scrub across the centre, true Sahara sand and bare rock in the north, and greener savanna with acacia and doum palms in the far south.

TF.extra: A group of sub-Antarctic islands with no permanent population beyond small scientific bases, no public road network and no street-level imagery.

TG.roads: Drives on the right. Signage is in French, the coastal trunk road has white markings and black-and-white painted kerbs, and inland roads are red laterite with speed bumps at every village.
TG.poles: Concrete poles in Lome and wooden poles inland.
TG.built: Concrete block houses with corrugated iron roofs, French-influenced administrative buildings in Lome, and fortified mud tower houses with conical thatch in the Tamberma valley in the north.
TG.nature: Red-orange laterite soil, oil palm, teak and mango near the coast, and drier savanna with baobab and shea further north.
TG.extra: Yellow-shirted motorcycle taxis and swarms of scooters, with petrol sold from glass bottles at the roadside.

TH.plates: White plates with black characters and the province name in Thai along the bottom; taxis and commercial vehicles use yellow plates with black characters.
TH.roads: Drives on the left. Broken white centre lines with wide white edge lines, kerbs painted in alternating red and white where parking is banned and black and white elsewhere, and green motorway signs with Thai above English.
TH.poles: Square concrete poles with a tapering profile, extremely common and usually carrying dense bundles of overhead cable.
TH.built: Corrugated metal roofs, open-fronted concrete shophouses with rolling shutters, and temple roofs in gold and coloured glazed tile with sharp upturned finials.
TH.nature: Rice paddy, banana and coconut palms, rubber and oil palm in the south, and dense green secondary forest on the hills.
TH.extra: Spirit houses on small pillars outside homes and businesses are near-universal and a strong giveaway, along with pickup trucks with rear canopies and 7-Eleven shopfronts.

TJ.plates: White plates with black characters and a blue band on the left showing TJ and the flag, with a two-digit region code at the start.
TJ.roads: Drives on the right. Newly resurfaced main corridors with fresh white markings alongside very rough mountain tracks, blue direction signs, frequent tunnels, and only patchy guardrail above steep drops.
TJ.poles: Grey concrete poles along main roads, with timber poles and improvised supports in mountain villages.
TJ.built: Single-storey mud brick and rendered houses with shallow painted metal roofs behind walled courtyards, blue-painted gates and window frames, and Soviet apartment blocks in Dushanbe.
TJ.nature: Very steep bare brown and grey Pamir and Fann slopes with little cover, poplar and willow along rivers, apricot and mulberry around villages, and green irrigated valley floors.
TJ.extra: Large billboard portraits of the president appear beside roads and at town entrances with unusual frequency. Tree trunks are whitewashed to about a metre, and Opel and Mercedes saloons are common.

TK.extra: Three tiny atolls with no airport, only a few hundred metres of concrete path between village houses, almost no motor vehicles and no street-level imagery.

TL.plates: White plates with black characters, with government and international organisation vehicles carrying their own codes and marks.
TL.roads: Drives on the left. Narrow, often badly broken roads with no markings and no guardrail, with landslip damage and river crossings frequent in the hills; the few signs are in Portuguese and Tetum.
TL.poles: Concrete poles along the main coast road, with timber poles and very sparse distribution inland.
TL.built: Simple rendered block houses with corrugated metal or palm-thatch roofs, some Portuguese colonial buildings with arcades and tiled roofs in Dili, and traditional tall-roofed sacred houses in villages.
TL.nature: Steep dry hills with eucalyptus and scattered scrub, coconut palms along the coast, wide stony dry riverbeds, and red-brown eroded soil.
TL.extra: Catholic churches, roadside crucifixes and statues of the Virgin Mary are common and contrast sharply with neighbouring Indonesia. Traffic is light, with motorbikes, Indonesian minibuses and aid-agency Land Cruisers.

TM.plates: White plates with black characters and a region letter code; layouts have changed and older Soviet-style plates persist on rural vehicles.
TM.roads: Drives on the right. Long empty straight roads across desert with faded markings and no guardrail, contrasting with wide, immaculate, heavily lit boulevards in Ashgabat.
TM.built: Ashgabat is unmistakable: rank after rank of white marble-clad buildings with gold detailing, fountains and monumental arches. Outside the capital, low rendered single-storey houses with flat or shallow roofs behind courtyard walls.
TM.nature: Karakum sand and gravel desert with saxaul scrub and dunes, irrigated cotton along canals, and the bare Kopet Dag ridge on the Iranian border.
TM.extra: Imagery is very scarce. White cars strongly predominate in the capital, and monumental statues, portraits and empty plazas are recurring features.

TN.plates: White plates with black characters carrying the Arabic word تونس between two groups of digits, which is a reliable giveaway.
TN.roads: Drives on the right. Signs are bilingual Arabic and French, motorway panels are green, and kerbstones and tree trunks are frequently painted white.
TN.poles: Slim concrete poles in the towns with steel lattice pylons across open country.
TN.built: Whitewashed walls with blue doors, shutters and window grilles in the north and along the coast, flat roofs, and sand-coloured render inland with ksar and troglodyte dwellings in the south.
TN.nature: Olive groves in dead-straight rows over pale brown soil, cypress and eucalyptus windbreaks, cork oak in the north-west, and salt flats and date palms in the south.
TN.extra: Yellow taxis in Tunis, white louage shared minibuses with a coloured stripe along the side, and French shop signs beside Arabic ones.

TO.roads: Drives on the left, with a very low speed limit of around 50 kilometres per hour even on open roads. Tongatapu is almost entirely flat, so roads run dead straight between plantations with little marking.
TO.poles: Concrete and wooden poles along the main roads carrying low lines.
TO.built: Simple single-storey houses in concrete block or timber with metal roofs, and very numerous churches of competing denominations, often by far the largest building in a village.
TO.nature: Coconut plantations in regular grid rows, banana and yam gardens, flat coral limestone terrain and no rivers at all.
TO.extra: Pigs roam freely on and beside the road, which is a classic Tongan sight. Many people wear a woven ta ovala mat around the waist.

TR.plates: White plates with black characters and a narrow blue band on the left carrying TR and the flag, starting with a province number from 01 to 81.
TR.roads: Drives on the right. Motorway signs are blue and state highway signs green, both with white text; roads are wide and well surfaced with crisp markings and long runs of guardrail, and dual carriageways are the norm between towns.
TR.poles: Concrete poles in towns and steel lattice masts along highways, with tall transmission towers crossing the Anatolian plateau.
TR.built: Five- to ten-storey concrete apartment blocks with rendered facades and shallow red pantile roofs, almost all fitted with white or black solar water-heater tanks, and a mosque with one or two pencil minarets in every settlement.
TR.nature: Dry brown-yellow steppe and wheat on the central plateau, pine and maquis along the Mediterranean, olive and fig in the west, and green wooded mountains along the Black Sea.
TR.extra: Roof-mounted solar water heaters and frequent Turkish flags and Atatürk portraits are constant. Tractors and small pickups share rural roads, and roadside tea gardens with plastic chairs are ubiquitous.

TT.plates: White plates with black characters, with the leading letter coding the class: P for private cars, H for hired and taxi vehicles, T for goods vehicles.
TT.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Main highways are multi-lane with white markings, concrete barriers and overhead gantries around Port of Spain, while rural roads are narrow with deep concrete drains and heavy speed bumps.
TT.poles: Wooden utility poles carrying bundled cables are usual.
TT.built: Concrete block houses with galvanised metal roofs and burglar-barred windows, often part-finished with exposed columns; Port of Spain has gingerbread timber houses around the Queen's Park Savannah.
TT.nature: The forested Northern Range rises behind a flat central plain of sugar cane, rice and pasture; immortelle trees flower orange in the dry season, and mangrove and oil and gas infrastructure mark the south and west coasts.
TT.extra: English and Trinidadian Creole signage; Hindu jhandi prayer flags and mandirs beside mosques and churches, roti and doubles stalls at the roadside, and maxi-taxi minibuses striped by route colour.

TV.roads: Drives on the left. Funafuti has one short sealed road along the atoll with hardly any cars, mostly motorcycles, and no lane markings.
TV.poles: Short concrete poles along the single road.
TV.built: Small concrete and timber houses with corrugated-iron roofs, large rainwater tanks beside almost every building, and a few larger government and church buildings.
TV.nature: Coconut palms and pandanus on a very narrow strip of coral sand, with the calm lagoon on one side and ocean surf on the other.
TV.extra: The airport runway doubles as the island's main public space, used for sport and socialising whenever no aircraft is due.

TW.plates: White plates with black characters, typically three letters then four digits, with yellow plates on large trucks and buses and small plates on scooters.
TW.roads: Drives on the right. Vast numbers of scooters, with dedicated scooter waiting boxes painted ahead of the stop line at junctions and hook-turn boxes for two-stage left turns. Expressway signage is blue and white in traditional characters with romanisation.
TW.poles: Concrete utility poles carrying banks of transformers and thick tangles of cable, often leaning, with wires crossing the street repeatedly.
TW.built: Narrow four to six storey buildings faced in small ceramic tiles, with barred windows, rooftop water tanks and corrugated metal rooftop extensions, and vertically stacked shop signs on the facades.
TW.nature: Steep forested mountains rising abruptly behind the western plain, betel nut palms in dense straight rows, rice paddies, bamboo and banyan.
TW.extra: Traditional Chinese characters throughout, temples with elaborate swooping tiled roofs and ceramic dragons, and 7-Eleven and FamilyMart stores on almost every block.

TZ.plates: Yellow plates front and rear with black characters, starting with the letter T followed by three digits and three letters.
TZ.roads: Drives on the left. Trunk roads are good tarmac with a white broken centre line and yellow edge lines, with speed humps and rumble strips through every settlement and frequent police speed traps.
TZ.poles: Slim concrete poles with a visible casting seam along main roads, plus wooden poles in rural areas.
TZ.built: Concrete block and coral-rag walls under corrugated iron, Swahili coastal architecture with carved doors and whitewash in Zanzibar and Bagamoyo, and mud-and-pole huts with thatch inland.
TZ.nature: Red-brown to orange soil, acacia savanna and baobabs, sisal plantations, coconut and mango on the coast, and banana and maize on the highland slopes.
TZ.extra: Dala dala minibuses with painted route boards, Vodacom and Airtel red kiosks, and Swahili wording on shopfronts and roadside signs.

UA.plates: White plate with a blue strip on the left carrying the yellow-and-blue flag and UA; the format is two letters, four digits, two letters.
UA.roads: Direction signs are green on major routes and blue elsewhere, following the Soviet standard. Markings are white and often worn, many secondary roads are heavily patched or broken, and tree trunks along the verge are whitewashed.
UA.poles: Round tapered spun-concrete poles and square concrete posts are everywhere, frequently leaning, with wooden poles on older village lines.
UA.built: Soviet panel blocks in the towns and low village houses rendered white or pale blue with green-painted metal roofs, decorated gates and low fences. Orthodox churches carry gold or blue domes.
UA.nature: Very flat steppe and farmland with deep black chernozem soil, vast sunflower and wheat fields, rows of poplar and acacia along the roads, and birch and pine in the north.
UA.extra: Ukrainian Cyrillic uses і, ї, є and ґ, which distinguishes it from Russian at a glance. Concrete bus shelters with mosaic panels, АТБ supermarket signs and roadside memorials are common; domains end in .ua.

UG.plates: White front and yellow rear plates with black characters, format U then two letters, three digits and a letter. Government vehicles use red plates with white characters.
UG.roads: Drives on the left. Main roads are tarmac with a white centre line and yellow edge lines, black-and-white painted kerbs, and very frequent speed humps through trading centres.
UG.poles: Slim concrete poles along main roads and wooden poles in rural areas.
UG.built: Red fired-brick buildings with rusty corrugated iron roofs, long terraces of unrendered brick lock-up shops, and shopfronts painted in telecom colours.
UG.nature: Deep red laterite soil, banana plantations everywhere, tall elephant grass at the roadside, eucalyptus stands, and lush green cover almost year round.
UG.extra: Boda boda motorcycle taxis in enormous numbers, MTN yellow and Airtel red paint on nearly every kiosk, and long-horned Ankole cattle in the west.

UM.extra: A scattered group of uninhabited or minimally staffed islands and atolls, mostly wildlife refuges or former military sites, with no civilian population, no public roads and no street-level imagery.

US.plates: Plates are issued per state, most often white or pale with the state name across the top and frequently a slogan, graphic or coloured background. Around twenty states require a rear plate only.
US.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Yellow lines separate opposing traffic while white lines separate same-direction lanes and mark edges; stop signs are red octagons reading STOP, warning signs yellow diamonds and guide signs green. Traffic signals commonly hang from mast arms or span wires over the junction.
US.poles: Tall wooden poles with horizontal crossarms, cylindrical transformers and heavy cable bundles line most roads; concrete and steel poles are common in Florida and parts of the south-west.
US.built: Timber-framed houses with vinyl or clapboard siding and asphalt shingle roofs on open lawns without boundary walls, plus single-storey commercial strips set behind deep parking lots with tall pole signs.
US.nature: Enormously varied: deciduous hardwood and loblolly pine in the east, red clay soil in the south-east, grain prairie through the centre, sagebrush and saguaro desert in the south-west, and conifer forest in the north-west.
US.extra: English signage with .com addresses; yellow school buses, pickup trucks, fire hydrants, kerbside US Postal Service mailboxes with a red flag, and national chain branding at nearly every interchange.

UY.plates: Mercosur plates: white with a blue strip across the top reading URUGUAY. The previous generation was colour-coded by department, with Montevideo issuing dark blue plates with white characters.
UY.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Centre lines are generally white with white edge lines, on flat and lightly trafficked roads; rural junctions are marked with simple white-painted posts and plain direction signs.
UY.poles: Square and round concrete poles are common in towns, with long runs of wooden poles across the open countryside.
UY.built: Low single-storey houses with flat or shallow roofs, rendered and painted, built to the pavement edge around a grid plaza; corrugated metal and brick farm buildings out in the country.
UY.nature: Gently rolling grassland cuchillas grazed by cattle and sheep, with planted blocks of eucalyptus and pine, solitary ombu trees, no mountains at all, and dunes and pine along the Atlantic coast.
UY.extra: Rioplatense Spanish. Every filling station is ANCAP, which is an instant giveaway, and people carrying a thermos flask and mate gourd under the arm are a common street sight.

UZ.plates: White plates with black characters, opening with a two-digit region number in a separate box on the left and a blue UZ band with the flag on the right.
UZ.roads: Drives on the right. Blue direction signs with white text, worn white markings on older concrete-slab highways, and avenues of poplars planted tight to the carriageway on rural roads.
UZ.poles: Grey concrete poles, square or round, closely spaced along roads, with lattice towers crossing the cotton plains.
UZ.built: Soviet panel blocks and wide boulevards in the cities, single-storey mud-brick and rendered houses behind blank street walls in villages, and turquoise-tiled domes and madrasa portals in the historic towns.
UZ.nature: Irrigated cotton and wheat fields with canals and poplar windbreaks, dry steppe and desert to the west, and green mountain foothills in the east.
UZ.extra: Nearly every car is a white locally built Chevrolet, which is one of the strongest single-country tells anywhere. Many vehicles are converted to run on gas, with cylinders visible in boots.

VA.plates: White plate with black characters prefixed SCV, or CV on privately held vehicles; no EU strip.
VA.roads: The few roads are narrow and enclosed by walls, with squares and approaches paved in small black basalt setts laid in fan patterns. Vehicle access is controlled and signage is minimal.
VA.built: Travertine and marble Renaissance and Baroque architecture at monumental scale, a vast colonnaded square, and ochre-rendered service buildings with green shutters behind the main facades.
VA.nature: Formal clipped gardens with umbrella pines, palms, cypress and box hedging; there is no open countryside at all.
VA.extra: Signage is in Italian with Latin inscriptions carved on the monuments. Swiss Guards in striped uniforms, yellow-and-white flags and yellow post boxes are visible, and Street View coverage is limited to the square and a few approaches.

VC.plates: White plates with black characters and a leading letter marking the vehicle class.
VC.roads: Traffic drives on the left. Narrow, steep coastal roads with sharp bends and minimal markings, concrete drains at the verge, and short concrete-paved sections on the steepest climbs.
VC.built: Small concrete-block houses with corrugated metal roofs terraced into hillsides, painted in strong colours, behind stone or block retaining walls.
VC.nature: A steep volcanic spine rising to La Soufriere under rainforest, with banana and arrowroot plots on the lower slopes, coconut palms on the leeward coast and black volcanic sand beaches; the Grenadines by contrast are low, dry and scrubby.
VC.extra: English signage, East Caribbean dollar prices, and brightly painted private minibuses with slogans across the windscreen.

VE.plates: White plates with black characters and a band across the top reading VENEZUELA with the flag, in mixed letter and digit formats.
VE.roads: Traffic drives on the right. Markings are frequently faded or missing entirely, and the wide autopistas have concrete central barriers in poor repair, potholes and missing drain covers.
VE.poles: Round and square concrete poles carry the distribution network, with wooden poles in rural areas.
VE.built: Concrete block and red brick houses, much of it unrendered, stacked densely up hillsides above the cities; mid-century modernist concrete public buildings and slab blocks in Caracas.
VE.nature: Flat llanos grassland with palms and cattle in the interior, a green coastal mountain range above the Caribbean, dry cactus scrub in the north-west, and flat-topped tepui mesas in the far south.
VE.extra: Spanish signage; political murals and Chavez imagery are widespread, PDVSA is the only petrol brand, queues at fuel stations are common, and a high proportion of 1980s and 1990s American cars are still running.

VG.plates: White plates with black characters carrying the words British Virgin Islands.
VG.roads: Drives on the left even though nearly every vehicle is a left-hand-drive American import. Roads on Tortola are extremely steep and narrow with tight switchbacks over the central ridge, and the steepest grades are surfaced in grooved concrete rather than asphalt.
VG.poles: Wooden poles heavily guyed on the slopes, with cables sagging across the hairpins.
VG.built: Concrete houses with red or green metal roofs stepped up the hillsides on tall foundation piers, plus low commercial buildings in Road Town.
VG.nature: Steep dry hills with scrub, turpentine trees and cactus, white beaches below, and a constant view of other islands across the Sir Francis Drake Channel.
VG.extra: US dollars and American shops combined with British road markings and left-hand traffic; charter yachts are moored in almost every bay.

VI.plates: US-sized plates reading US Virgin Islands, commonly with the American Paradise slogan.
VI.roads: Drives on the left, uniquely among United States jurisdictions, using left-hand-drive American vehicles. Roads on St Thomas are steep, narrow and heavily potholed, with American sign shapes and speed limits in miles per hour.
VI.poles: American-pattern wooden poles with drum transformers, heavily guyed on the slopes.
VI.built: Danish colonial arcaded buildings in yellow, red and ochre with green shutters in Charlotte Amalie and Christiansted, linked by stepped step-streets, with concrete hillside villas and white roof cisterns above.
VI.nature: Steep dry hills with scrub and turpentine trees, flamboyant trees in flower, and white beaches full of charter yachts.
VI.extra: US road signs, mainland chain stores and the US Postal Service alongside Danish street names such as Dronningens Gade and Kongens Gade, with traffic on the left.

VN.plates: Private vehicles use white plates with black characters, commercial vehicles yellow with black, state vehicles blue with white and military red with white. The number starts with a two-digit provincial code.
VN.roads: Drives on the right. White edge and lane lines with yellow used on some newer highways, blue and green direction signs in Vietnamese with diacritics, and low concrete bollards and kerb blocks separating motorbike lanes.
VN.poles: Round and square concrete poles carrying enormous tangled bundles of cable looped between them, one of the most recognisable street textures in the region.
VN.built: Narrow tube houses three to six storeys tall and only three or four metres wide, with ornate painted facades, balconies and decorative rooflines, packed shoulder to shoulder along every road.
VN.nature: Bright green rice paddy on the deltas, limestone karst hills in the north, red basalt soil and coffee in the central highlands, and casuarina and coconut along the coast.
VN.extra: Red banners with yellow lettering, hammer-and-sickle and national flags, and blue rectangular street name signs are everywhere. Motorbike traffic is overwhelming and conical hats are still common in rural areas.

VU.roads: Drives on the right, which is unusual for Melanesia and a useful separator from Fiji and the Solomons. Port Vila has kerbed sealed streets and the Efate ring road is sealed, while other islands have coral and mud tracks.
VU.poles: Concrete poles in and around Port Vila and Luganville, thinning to nothing in rural areas.
VU.built: Concrete and timber buildings with metal roofs, French-influenced shopfronts and awnings in Port Vila, and traditional thatched nakamal meeting houses in villages.
VU.nature: Dense green bush with huge banyan trees, coconut plantations, and black volcanic sand beaches on Tanna and Ambrym.
VU.extra: Signage mixes French and English with Bislama, an unusual combination in the Pacific and the clearest Vanuatu tell.

WF.roads: Drives on the right. A narrow sealed road rings Wallis with very little traffic, French-pattern signs and low speed limits, and Futuna has a rougher coastal road.
WF.poles: Concrete poles along the ring road.
WF.built: Very large, elaborately decorated Catholic churches dominate small villages of simple metal-roofed houses, alongside traditional oval fale with thatched roofs and open sides.
WF.nature: Coconut palms and dense low bush, green crater lakes in the interior of Wallis, and a wide shallow lagoon with small motu islets offshore.
WF.extra: French signage and CFP franc prices in an intensely Catholic Polynesian setting, with the basilica at Mata-Utu and the shrine at Poi on Futuna as landmarks.

WS.roads: Drives on the left, having switched sides in 2009, so the traffic mixes right-hand-drive Japanese imports with older left-hand-drive American vehicles. Coast roads are smooth sealed two-lane with white edge lines and frequent speed humps through villages.
WS.poles: Concrete poles along the main coast roads, evenly spaced and in good condition.
WS.built: Every village has open-sided oval fale on a raised platform with rows of pillars and a domed thatch or corrugated roof, alongside very large, brightly painted churches that dwarf the houses.
WS.nature: Coconut palms, breadfruit and taro plantations, lush green volcanic interior, and black lava fields reaching the road on Savaii.
WS.extra: Tiled family tombs stand in the front gardens right beside the road, which is a strong Samoan giveaway. Villages enforce evening curfews marked by a gong.

XK.plates: White plates with black characters in a digits-digits-letters layout, with a blue band on the left carrying the code RKS. In the Serb-majority north you also see Serbian plates.
XK.roads: Drives on the right. Newly built motorways with bright green signage and fresh concrete barriers contrast sharply with narrow, patched two-lane roads lined with car washes, tyre shops and petrol stations.
XK.poles: Concrete poles, frequently leaning, with untidy bundles of cable and low-hanging lines.
XK.built: Large unfinished houses of three or four storeys in red brick and bare concrete with rebar sticking out of the top floor and steep red-tiled roofs, standing beside completed neighbours; slim minarets and Orthodox churches.
XK.nature: Rolling arable farmland with maize, small haystacks and lines of poplars, backed by bare limestone mountains along the western and southern edges.
XK.extra: Albanian and Kosovan flags flown together with American flags, roadside memorials to the 1999 war, and KFOR military vehicles and signage.

YE.roads: Drives on the right. Mostly narrow and poorly maintained roads with faded or absent markings, no guardrail on mountain sections, and frequent checkpoints and earth berms.
YE.built: Tall multi-storey tower houses of mud brick or stone with white gypsum tracery around windows are the signature of Sana'a and the highlands; stone villages sit on ridge tops and flat-roofed mud buildings dominate elsewhere.
YE.nature: Steeply terraced arid mountains with qat and coffee on the terraces, bare rock and dust, sand desert to the east, and scattered acacia in the lowlands.
YE.extra: Coverage is extremely limited and largely from handheld or vehicle-mounted photography. Older Toyota Land Cruisers and pickups make up most traffic.

YT.plates: French plates: white with black characters, a blue EU strip with F, and the department number 976 in the right-hand band.
YT.roads: Drives on the right. A single narrow sealed road loops Grande-Terre with French signage, many speed humps and constant pedestrians on the verge, and traffic backs up badly on the approach to Mamoudzou.
YT.poles: Concrete poles along the coast road, with cables strung across steep gullies.
YT.built: Breeze-block and corrugated-iron housing packed onto steep hillsides, much of it informal, with green and white mosque minarets in almost every village and French public buildings in the towns.
YT.nature: Lush green hills with mango, ylang-ylang and baobab trees, mangrove creeks, and a very wide shallow barrier-reef lagoon offshore.
YT.extra: French signage and euro prices in a visibly Comorian Muslim society, with women wearing brightly coloured salouva and pale msindzano face paste.

ZA.plates: White plates with black characters whose format varies by province, such as three letters, three digits and GP for Gauteng, or a CA-type three-letter code in the Western Cape, many with a small provincial emblem.
ZA.roads: Drives on the left. A white centre line with a yellow edge line marking a wide shoulder that slow vehicles pull into, blue or green direction signage, and steel armco barriers on white-tipped posts.
ZA.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms on rural roads, concrete poles and tall steel lighting columns in town, and very tall high-mast floodlights standing over townships.
ZA.built: Face-brick suburban houses with tiled pitched roofs behind walls topped with electric fencing, dense corrugated iron shacks in townships, and low shopping centres with large car parks.
ZA.nature: Highveld grassland that turns gold and brown in winter, fynbos and vineyards in the Cape, red and grey soils, eucalyptus and pine plantations, and aloes on road cuttings.
ZA.extra: White Toyota Quantum minibus taxis are everywhere, informal traders work the verges, and highveld air is unusually clear with a low hard sun.

ZM.plates: White plates with black characters, usually three letters then four digits, with newer issues carrying a blue band on the left.
ZM.roads: Drives on the left. Long straight tarmac with a white centre line and yellow edge lines, black-and-white painted kerbs and bollards in towns, and frequent police checkpoints marked with cones.
ZM.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms are common, with concrete poles near the towns and lattice pylons along the Copperbelt corridor.
ZM.built: Concrete block and fired-brick houses with corrugated iron roofs, low shopping parades with deep verandas, and Shoprite-anchored strip malls in the larger towns.
ZM.nature: Miombo woodland of fairly uniform medium-height trees over reddish-brown soil, tall termite mounds, maize fields, and open dambo grassland in the flats.
ZM.extra: Blue-and-white minibuses, Airtel red and MTN yellow kiosks, and heavy articulated lorry traffic hauling copper on the main corridors.

ZW.plates: White plates with black characters, typically three letters then four digits.
ZW.roads: Drives on the left. Narrow tarmac with a white centre line and yellow edge lines, badly worn surfaces with potholes and patching, and police roadblocks with cones and stop signs.
ZW.poles: Wooden poles with cross-arms along most roads, with concrete poles in the towns.
ZW.built: Face-brick and rendered houses with corrugated iron or tiled roofs, colonial-era shopping verandas in small towns, and wide jacaranda-lined avenues in Harare.
ZW.nature: Msasa woodland that flushes red and orange in spring, granite kopjes and balancing boulders, red-brown soil, and maize and tobacco fields across the highveld.
ZW.extra: A high proportion of very old vehicles and Japanese used imports, with Econet branding on shops and kiosks.
